**Surah al-Hadid**
It has twenty-nine verses and is Meccan.

In the Name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

In the Name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** Tasbih (glorification, i.e. declaring Allah far exalted above any imperfection) means removing Allah, the Exalted, far from every evil. Likewise taqdis (sanctification) comes from the expressions "sabaha fi al-ma'" (he swam in the water) and "qadasa fi al-ard" (he went far off into the land), meaning he went into it and moved far away.

Know that glorifying Allah from every evil includes removing from Him evil in His essence, in His attributes, in His acts, in His names, and in His rulings.

As for the essence: He must not be a locus of contingency (imkan), since evil is non-existence and its possibility. Negating contingency entails negating multiplicity, and negating multiplicity entails negating corporeality and accidentality, negating any opposite or equal, and affirming absolute unity.

As for the attributes: He must be free of ignorance, meaning He must encompass all known things, be able over all possible things, and His attributes must be free of change.

As for the acts: His act of bringing into existence must not depend on a matter and a pattern (mithal), because every matter and pattern is itself His act, as we have shown that everything other than Him is contingent, and every contingent thing is His act. If His acting depended on a matter and a pattern, this would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul). It must also not depend on time and place, because every time is composed of parts that pass away, so it is contingent; and every place is considered contingent, composed of individual spaces (ahyaz). Thus each of them is contingent and originated. If His acting depended on time and place, the acting of time and place would depend on further time and place, leading to an infinite regress. It must also not depend on bringing about benefit or averting harm, for otherwise He would be perfected by another and deficient in His essence, and that is impossible.

As for the names: as He said, ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ (al-A'raf 7:180).

As for the rulings: that everything He legislates is a public good (maslaha), a kindness, and good, and that His bestowing it is a favor and a good, not something obligatory upon Him but by way of kindness. In summary, it must be known from this principle that His rule and obligation bind everyone, that no one has any ruling or obligation over Him, and that nothing is owed to anyone by Him at all. This is the foundation of the principles of tasbih.

**The second issue:** In some openings (of surahs) the verb appears in the past tense, "sabbaha", and in others in the present tense, "yusabbihu". This indicates that these things' being glorifiers is not restricted to one time over another; rather they have been glorifying Allah forever in the past,

[Page 180]

and will be glorifying Him forever in the future. This is because their being glorifiers is an attribute necessarily inherent in their quiddities (mahiyyat), so it is impossible for those quiddities to be separated from that glorification. We said that this being-glorifying is a necessary attribute of their quiddities because everything other than the Necessary Existent is contingent, and every contingent thing is dependent on the Necessary Existent. The Necessary Existent's being necessary requires that He be declared free of every evil in essence, attributes, acts, rulings, and names, as we have explained. Thus it becomes clear that this being-glorifying was present in the past and will be present in the future. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** This verb is sometimes transitive with the preposition lam, as in this surah, and sometimes directly transitive, as in His saying, ﴿and glorify Him morning and evening﴾ (al-Fath 48:9). Originally it is transitive directly, because the meaning of "sabbahtuhu" is "I removed him far from evil." So the lam is either like the lam in "nasahtuhu" and "nasahtu lahu" (I advised him), or it means "yusabbihu li-Allah" (glorifies for Allah), that is, he initiated the glorification for the sake of Allah and sincerely for His countenance.

**The fourth issue:** Al-Zajjaj claimed that the intended glorification here is the glorification that is speech, and he argued for this with two points:

The first: He, the Exalted, said, ﴿There is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ (al-Isra' 17:44). Had the intended meaning of glorification been the indication of the traces of creation upon the Creator, they would have understood it.

The second: He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with Dawud﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:79). If glorification were an expression for the indication of creation upon the Creator, there would be no specification of Dawud, peace be upon him, in that.

Know that this argument is weak for two reasons:

As for the first: the indication of these bodies upon the sanctification of Allah's essence, His attributes, and His acts is among the most subtle indications, and that is why rational people differed about it. So His saying, ﴿but you do not understand﴾, may be an allusion to peoples who were ignorant of this indication. Also, His saying, ﴿you do not understand﴾, if it is not an allusion to a specific group, is addressed to all, as though He had said: all of these did not understand that, and that does not preclude that some of them understood it.

As for the second argument: it is weak because it is possible that Allah created life in the mountain so that it spoke the glorification. However, the inanimate objects that we know by necessity to be inanimate, it is impossible to say that they glorify Allah by way of speech with that glorification, because if we allowed that a well-made act could proceed from inanimate things, we could not use the acts of Allah, the Exalted, as evidence that He is knowing and living. That would be disbelief. Rather, the truth is that glorification which is speech proceeds only from a rational being who knows Allah, the Exalted, so that by that speech he intends the declaration of his Lord's freedom from imperfection, and such a thing is not valid from inanimate objects. So the general glorification that results from both rational beings and inanimate things must be interpreted in one of two ways:

The first: they glorify in the sense that they indicate His exaltation and freedom from imperfection.

The second: that all possible things are wholly submissive to Him; He disposes of them as He wills, and there is no preventer or repeller of His act and His bringing into being.

Once you have understood this premise, we say: if we take the glorification mentioned in the verse to be glorification by speech, then by His saying, ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, is meant whoever is in the heavens, including the bearers of the Throne: ﴿But if they are arrogant, those with your Lord glorify Him﴾ (Fussilat 41:38), and among them are those brought near (to Allah): ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You; You are our Protector, not them"﴾ (Saba' 34:41). As for the glorifiers who are on earth, among them are the prophets, as Dhu al-Nun said: ﴿There is no deity except You; glory be to You﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:87), and Musa said: ﴿Glory be to You; I have repented to You﴾ (al-A'raf 7:143). And the Companions glorify, as He said: ﴿Glory be to You; protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:191).

But if we take this glorification to be the glorification in the figurative sense, then the parts of the heavens, the particles of the earth, the mountains, the sands, the seas, the trees, the animals, Paradise, the Fire, the Throne, the Footstool, the Preserved Tablet, the Pen, light, darkness, essences, attributes, bodies, and accidents, all of them, are glorifiers, humbled, submissive, subject to the majesty of Allah, yielding to the disposal of Allah, as the Mighty, the One who speaks, said: ﴿There is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾ (al-Isra' 17:44). This glorification is what is meant by prostration in His saying, ﴿To Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:15).

As for His saying, ﴿and He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾: the meaning is that He is the Powerful whom nothing can contest. So "the Mighty" points to perfection of power, and "the Wise" points to His being the Knowing, from whose knowledge nothing is hidden, of particulars or universals; or it means He is the One who performs His acts in accordance with wisdom and rightness. Since knowing that He is powerful takes precedence over knowing that He is knowing, He rightly placed "the Mighty" before "the Wise" in the mention.

Know that His saying, ﴿and He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾, indicates that the Mighty is none other than Him, because this form (of exclusive predication) conveys restriction. One says, "Zayd is the scholar, not anyone else." This entails that there is no deity except the One, because anything other than Him is neither Mighty nor Wise, and whatever is not like that is not a deity.

Know that the true King is the One who is self-sufficient in His essence and in all His attributes, independent of everything other than Him, while everything other than Him is in need of Him in both its essence and its attributes. The one described by these two qualities is none other than Him, glorified is He.

As for the claim that He is self-sufficient in His essence and in all His attributes, independent of everything other than Him: if His essence were in need of something else, He would be possible in His essence (mumkin li-dhatihi), and so would be originated (muhdath), and would not be necessary of existence (wajib al-wujud). As for the claim that He is self-sufficient in all His attributes, both negative and relational, independent of everything other than Him: every attribute that one supposes for Him is either such that His essence, glorified is He, is sufficient for its realization, whether the attribute is negative or affirmative, or it is not such that His essence is sufficient for it. If His essence is sufficient for it, then by the permanence of that essence there is the permanence of that attribute, whether it is negative or affirmative. If it is not sufficient for it, then His essence is not sufficient in itself, and then that essence becomes inseparable from the affirmation of that attribute or from its negation. Then the affirmation of that attribute and its negation depend on the affirmation of another matter and its negation. Whatever depends on what depends on a thing depends on that thing. So His essence, glorified is He, would depend for its realization on the realization of the cause of the affirmation of that attribute or the cause of its negation. Whatever depends on another is possible in its essence, so the one necessary of existence in its essence would be possible of existence in its essence. This is a contradiction. Thus it is established that He, glorified is He, is not in need of anything else, neither in His essence nor in any of His negative or affirmative attributes.

As for the claim that everything other than Him is in need of Him: everything other than Him is possible, because the necessary of existence cannot be more than one, and the possible必ず needs an effecting agent (mu'aththir), and there is no necessary of existence except this One. Therefore, everything other than Him is in need of Him, whether it is a substance (jawhar) or an accident ('arad), and whether the substance is spiritual (ruhani) or corporeal (jismani).

A group of rational thinkers held that the influence of the necessary of existence lies in bestowing existence, not in quiddities (mahiyyat). So the necessary of existence makes blackness exist, but it is impossible that it makes blackness to be blackness. They said: if the blackness's being blackness were by the agent, then it would follow from the supposition of the non-existence of that agent that blackness would not remain blackness, and this is impossible. It is said to them: on this premise it follows for you that existence is also not by the agent, for otherwise it would follow from the supposition of the non-existence of that agent that existence would not be existence. If they say: the influence of the agent is not on existence, but on making the quiddity described as existing, we say: this is refuted from two aspects.

The first: that the quiddity's being described as existing is not an affirmative matter (amr thubuti). For if it were an affirmative matter, it would have a quiddity and an existence, and then the quiddity's being described as existing would be an addition to it, and an infinite regress (tasalsul) would follow, which is impossible. And since the quiddity's being described with existence is not an affirmative matter, it is impossible to say: the agent has no influence on the quiddity nor on existence, but rather its influence is on the quiddity's being described with existence.

The second: on the supposition that this descriptive attribute is an affirmative matter, it is also impossible to make it an effect of the agent, for otherwise it would follow, on the supposition of the non-existence of that agent, that the descriptive attribute would remain a descriptive attribute. It has become clear that if the doubt they mentioned were sound and firmly established, it would follow that influence and the influencer are denied altogether. Rather, just as quiddities have become existent only through the influence of the necessary of existence, so too quiddities have become quiddities only through the influence of the necessary of existence. And when these truths become evident, the truth of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ becomes manifest by rational proof. Indeed, the dominion of the heavens and the earth, relative to the perfection of His dominion, is less than an atom; rather, it has no ratio whatsoever to the perfection of His dominion, because the dominion of the heavens and the earth is a finite dominion, while the perfection of His dominion is infinite, and the finite has absolutely no ratio to the infinite. But He, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the dominion of the heavens and the earth because it is a visible, perceptible thing, and most creatures have weak intellects, so they can rarely ascend from the perceptible to the intelligible.

* Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned among the signs of the horizons the dominion of the heavens and the earth, He mentioned after it the signs of the selves, saying: ﴿He gives life and causes death, and He is powerful over all things﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: The exegetes (mufassirun) mentioned two aspects regarding it:

One: He gives life to the dead for the resurrection, and causes the living to die in this world.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: He gives life to the drops of semen (nutfah), making them into persons who are rational, understanding, and speaking, and He causes death. But in my view there is a third aspect: the intended meaning is not that the giving of life and causing of death is restricted to a specific time and specific persons, but rather its meaning is that He is the One capable of creating life and death, as He said in Surat al-Mulk: ﴿Who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. The purpose of this is that He, glorified is He, is the One who alone brings into being these two quiddities absolutely, no obstacle prevents Him from them, and no repeller turns Him away from them. In that case, the two aspects that the exegetes mentioned are included in it.

The second issue: The position of ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is in the nominative case, with the meaning "He is the one who gives life and causes death." It is also permissible that it be in the accusative, with the meaning: "To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth while He is giving life and causing death." Know that when He, exalted is He, first mentioned the signs of the horizons, and second the signs of the selves, He mentioned a term that encompasses all, saying: ﴿And He is powerful over all things﴾. The benefits of this verse are mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Mulk.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward, and He is Knowing of all things.﴾ On this verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** It is related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said, explaining this verse: "He is the First, nothing is before Him, and the Last, nothing is after Him." Know that this station is awe-inspiring, obscure and profound, and the discussion of it has several aspects.

**First:** Precedence of one thing over another can be understood in several ways.

**One:** Precedence by influence. We understand that the movement of the finger has precedence over the movement of the ring. What is meant by this precedence is that the prior thing is the cause that influences the later one.

**Two:** Precedence by need, not by influence. We understand that two needs one, although we know that one is not the cause of two.

**Three:** Precedence by honour, such as the precedence of Abu Bakr over Umar.

**Four:** Precedence by rank. This is either from a sensible starting point, such as the precedence of the imam over the follower, or from an intelligible starting point. The latter is like when we take the starting point to be the highest genus: the more a species descends in lowness, the more it is later in order, and if we reverse this, the matter is reversed.

**Five:** Precedence by time. This is that what exists in a prior time has precedence over what exists in a later time. These are the divisions of priority and precedence that people of intellect have worked out. In my view, there is here a sixth kind, which is like the precedence of some parts of time over others. This precedence is not precedence by time, for otherwise time would have to encompass another time, and then the discussion of that encompassing time would be like the discussion of what it encompasses, so it would follow that every time is encompassed by another time without end, such that all of them are present in this now. Then this present now would not be one, but every present would be within another present without end, and that is not intelligible. Also, the totality of those present moments is later than the totality of past moments, so there would be another time encompassing the totality of times. But that is impossible, because since it is a time, it would be included in the totality of times. Then that time would be both included in that totality and outside of it, which is impossible. Thus it is clear by this manifest demonstration that the precedence of some parts of time over others is not by time. And it is clearly not by cause or by need, for otherwise they would exist together, just as cause and effect exist together, and one and two exist together. Nor is it by honour or by place. So it is established that the precedence of some parts of time over others is a sixth kind, different from the five kinds mentioned.

Knowing this, we say: the Qur'an indicates that He, exalted is He, is first before everything else, and demonstration also indicates this meaning. For we say: everything other than the Necessary Existent is contingent, and every contingent is originated, so everything other than the Necessary Existent is originated, and that Necessary Existent is first before everything else.

We said that everything other than the Necessary Existent is contingent because if two necessary existents by their essence were found, they would share in necessary existence in essence and be distinguished by specification, and what makes them share is other than what makes them distinct. So each of them would be composite. Then each of their two parts, if it is necessary, the two parts share in necessity and differ by specificity, so each of those two parts would also be composite, and an infinite regress would follow. And if they were not both necessary, or if one of them were not necessary, then the whole which is constituted by it would more fittingly not be necessary. Thus it is established that everything other than the Necessary Existent is contingent, and every contingent is originated, because every contingent is in need of an influencer. That need is either in the state of existence or in the state of non-existence. If it is in the state of existence, then either in the state of continuance, which is impossible, because it would require the bringing into being of what already exists and the obtaining of what is already obtained, which is impossible; or that need is in the state of origination or in the state of non-existence. On both assumptions it follows that every contingent is originated. Thus it is established that everything other than that Necessary Existent is originated and in need of that Necessary Existent. So that Necessary Existent is before everything else.

Then the intellect sought the manner of that precedence, and we said: that precedence cannot be by influence, because the influencer, insofar as it is an influencer, is related to the effect insofar as it is an effect, and two related things together are simultaneous, and simultaneity is not precedence. Nor can it be by mere need, because the one in need and the one needed may exist together, and we have shown that simultaneity is impossible here. Nor can it be by mere honour, for what is required from this precedence here is not merely that He, exalted is He, is more honourable than the contingent things. As for spatial precedence, it is invalid, and even if it were established, the precedence of the originator over the originated is a further matter beyond one of them being above the other in direction. As for temporal precedence, it is invalid, because time too is contingent and originated. First, because we have shown that the Necessary Existence cannot be more than one. Second, because the sign of contingency and origination is more evident in it, as in other things, since all its parts succeed one another, and whatever comes into being after non-existence and ceases after existence is undoubtedly contingent in its originator. And since all the parts of time are contingent and originated, and the whole is constituted by the parts, then what is in need of a contingent originated thing is more fittingly contingent and originated. So time, in its totality and in its parts, is contingent and originated. Therefore the precedence of its originator over it cannot be by time, for what precedes all times cannot be by time, otherwise it would follow that in that time it would be included in the totality of times, since it is a time, and also be outside them, since it is their container. And a container is other than what is contained, not identical with it. But for one thing to be both inside and outside another is impossible. Third, because the nature of time requires flow and renewal, and that requires being preceded by something else, while pre-eternity is incompatible with being preceded by something else. So combining them is impossible. Thus it is established that the precedence of the Creator over everything else is by no means by time. So what the intellect holds is that He precedes everything else, but that this precedence is not by any of these five modes. What remains is another kind of precedence, different from these five kinds. As for the manner of that precedence, the intellect has no report of it, because whatever occurs to the intellect must be accompanied by some state of time, and the proof has shown that all of that is impossible. So His being first is known in summary, but as for knowing it in detail and comprehending the reality of that firstness, the minds of creatures have no trace of it.

**Second type of the subtleties of this topic:** Pre-eternity (al-Azal) is prior to "always" (al-La yazal). Pre-eternity is nothing other than the Real. So the precedence of pre-eternity over "always" requires a distinction between pre-eternity and "always." This requires that "always" have a beginning and an end, so that this distinction is achieved. But supposing such an end is impossible, because every beginning you suppose, "always" was already present before it, since the beginning supposed before that supposed end by an addition of a hundred years belongs to the "always" and not to pre-eternity. So the meaning of "always" was existing before it was existing, and that is impossible.

**Third type of the subtleties of this topic:** The distinction of pre-eternity from "always" requires the termination of the reality of pre-eternity, and the termination of the reality of pre-eternity is impossible, because what has no beginning cannot end. And when its ending is impossible, it is impossible for the reality of "always" to come about after it. So the distinction of pre-eternity from "always," and of "always" from pre-eternity, is impossible, and when this distinction is impossible, precedence and posteriority are impossible.

So these are obscure investigations into the reality of precedence, firstness and eternity, and they arise only from the bewilderment of human minds in the light of the majesty of the reality of eternity and firstness. For the intellect only knows a thing when it encompasses it, and whatever the intellect conceives and stops at is encompassed by it, and what is encompassed is limited, while eternity lies outside that. So He, glorified is He, is outward and inward: as regards His being first, He is more manifest than every manifest thing in this respect, for intellects bear witness to the attribution of originated things to an originator who precedes them. So His, exalted is He, being first is more evident than every evident thing in this respect. Then when you want to know the reality of that firstness, you fail, because whatever your intellect and knowledge encompass is limited by your intellect and encompassed by your knowledge, and so it is finite, and firstness lies outside us. So His, exalted is He, being first, when considered in this respect, is more hidden than every hidden thing. This is the discussion of His, exalted is He, being first.

As for the discussion of His being last: some people said this is impossible, because He, exalted is He, would only be last to everything else if He remained when everything else had ceased to exist. But the ceasing of what is other than Him is only after its existence, and that after-ness is temporal. So it is not possible to suppose the non-existence of everything other than Him except with the existence of the time by which that after-ness is realised. Then the state of what is supposed to be the non-existence of everything other than Him is that not everything other than Him is non-existent. This is a contradiction. So supposing His remaining while everything other than Him ceases is impossible. This doubt is also based on the premise that precedence and posteriority are established only by time, and we have demonstrated the falsity of this premise, so this doubt is void.

As for those who admitted the possibility of the non-existence of everything other than Him while He continues, some of them made this necessary, so that His being last to all may be established. This is the doctrine of Jahm (Jahm ibn Safwan), for he claimed that He, glorified is He, conveys reward to the people of reward and conveys punishment to the people of punishment, then He annihilates Paradise and its people, Hellfire and its people, the Throne, the Footstool, the angels and the spheres, and nothing remains with God at all. Just as He existed in pre-eternity and nothing existed with Him, so nothing will remain existing in "always," for ever and ever, except Him. And this was argued against him with several arguments.

**First:** His saying "He is the Last," which would only be last in the sense of the annihilation of all.

**Second:** He, exalted is He, either knows the number of the movements of the people of Paradise and Hell, or He does not know them. If He knows them, He knows their quantity, and whatever has a determined number is finite. So the movements of the people of Paradise are finite. Then an eternal non-existence, not ending, must follow them. And if He does not know them, He is ignorant of them, and ignorance is impossible for God.

**Third:** Future events are capable of increase and decrease, and whatever is such is finite.

**The reply:** The possibility of the continuation of these things remains for ever. The proof of this is that if these quiddities lost their possibilities, the contingent by its essence would have to turn into the impossible by its essence. And if the power of God were to change from the capacity for influence into the impossibility of influence, then quiddities would change, and that is impossible. So this possibility must remain forever. Thus it is established that the termination of these originated things must be into pure non-existence. As for relying on the verse, we will mention the reply to it after this, God willing.

As for the second doubt, its reply is that He knows that these things have no determined number, and this is not ignorance. Ignorance is only that a thing has a determined number and one does not know it. But if a thing has no determined number and you know it as it is, this is not ignorance but knowledge.

As for the third objection, its answer is that what proceeds from Him into existence is never finite, in perpetuity. Furthermore, when the theologians (*mutakallimun*) established that the continuation of the world forever is possible, they relied, for the everlasting continuation of Paradise and Hell, on the consensus (*ijma'*) of the Muslims and on the apparent meanings of the verses. Its exposition is not hidden. As for the majority of Muslims who accepted that Paradise and Hell last forever, they differed over the meaning of His being ﴿the Last﴾ in several ways:

First: He, exalted is He, annihilates all the world and all contingent beings, so His being the Last is realized. Then He brings them back into existence and keeps them forever.

Second: The only existent that can validly be the last of all things is He. Since the validity of being the last of all things belongs exclusively to Him, glorified is He, He is therefore described as the Last.

Third: Existence proceeds from Him, exalted is He, beginning and continually descending until it reaches the last existent, which is the cause of everything other than itself and is not the cause of anything else. In this sense, the Truth, glorified is He, is the First. Then, when it has reached that point, it begins to ascend from this last existent step by step until it reaches the end of the ascent, and there is the existence of the Truth, glorified is He. Thus He, glorified is He, is the First in the descent of existence from Him to contingent beings, and the Last in the ascent from contingent beings to Him.

Fourth: He causes the creation to die and remains after them, so He, glorified is He, is the Last in this sense.

Fifth: He is the First in existence and the Last in inference (*istidlal*), because the purpose of all inferences is knowledge of the Creator. As for the rest of the inferences that do not aim at knowing the Creator, they are base and worthless. As for His being the Manifest and the Hidden: know that He is manifest in terms of existence, for you do not see any of the created or contingent things except that it is a proof of His existence, His subsistence, His reality, and His freedom from aspects of change, as we have established.

As for His being the Hidden, it is due to several aspects:

The first: the perfection of His being manifest is a cause of His being hidden. For if this sun were to remain on the sphere, we would not know that this light had come about through it. Rather, we might think that things shine by their own essence. But since it sets, and we see that whenever it sets the lights are extinguished and the illuminations vanish from this world, we then know that these lights come from the sun. Likewise, if the existence of God could be cut off from these contingent beings, it would then become clear that the existence of these contingent beings is from the existence of God, exalted is He. But since that bounty persists and is never cut off, its permanence and perfection become a cause of the occurrence of doubt, to the extent that one may think that the light of existence is not from Him, but that the existence of everything is from its own essence. Thus it becomes clear that this concealment has come about from the perfection of His existence and the permanence of His bounty. So glory be to Him who is hidden from the intellects because of the intensity of His manifestness, and veiled from them by the perfection of His light.

The second aspect: His quiddity (*mahiyyah*) is not at all comprehensible to humans. This is indicated by the fact that a person does not conceive the quiddity of a thing except when he perceives it either from his own self by way of direct awareness (*wijdan*), like pain, pleasure and the like, or perceives it by his senses, like colors, tastes and all other sensible things. As for that which is not like this, it is impossible for a person to conceive its quiddity at all. His specific identity, majestic is His majesty, is not like this, so it is not comprehensible to humans. It is also indicated by the fact that what is known of Him by creatures is either existence or negations, namely that He is not a body nor a substance; or relation, namely that He is the one who has such and such a function. The specific reality is different from these matters, so it is not comprehensible. It is also indicated by the fact that the most evident thing about Him to the intellect is that He is the Creator of these creatures and precedes them. You have already learned the bewilderment and perplexity of the intellect in knowing this priority. Thus it has become clear from what we have presented that He, glorified is He, is the First and the Last, and the Manifest and the Hidden.

I heard my father, may God have mercy on him, say: It is related that when this verse was revealed, the polytheists approached the House (the Ka'bah) and prostrated.

Second issue: Many scholars have used His saying ﴿He is the First﴾ as evidence that God is one. They said: "the First" is the singular precedent. For this reason, if someone says, "The first slave I buy is free," and then buys two slaves, neither is freed, because the condition of being first is the attainment of singularity, and here it has not been attained. If he then buys a single slave afterward, he does not free him either, because the condition of being first is that he be preceding, and here that has not been attained. Thus it is established that the condition for being first is being singular. Therefore the verse indicates that the Creator of the world is singular.

Third issue: Most exegetes said: He is the First because He is before everything; He is the Last because He is after everything; He is the Manifest according to the proofs; and He is the Hidden from the senses, veiled from the eyes. Some people, when they were unable to answer Jahm, said: The meaning of these expressions is like the saying of a speaker: "So-and-so is the first of this affair, its last, its manifest and its hidden," meaning: on him it turns, and by him it is completed.

Know that since it is possible to interpret the verse according to the aspects we have mentioned, while Jahm's argument is thereby refuted, we have no need to interpret the verse according to this figurative sense. They mentioned regarding "the Manifest" and "the Hidden" that the Manifest is the one who prevails and is exalted over everything. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they became victorious﴾ [al-Saff: 14], meaning: prevailing and exalted, from your saying, "I prevailed over so-and-so," meaning I rose above him. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and upon which they ascend﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33]. This is the meaning of what is narrated in the hadith: "You are the Manifest, so there is nothing above You." As for the Hidden, al-Zajjaj said: He is the one who knows what is hidden, as one says: "So-and-so suspects the affair of so-and-so," meaning he knows his inner circumstances. Al-Layth said: It is said: "You are more knowledgeable of the inner workings of this matter than so-and-so," meaning you are more informed of its inner aspect. So the meaning of His being the Hidden is His being knowledgeable of the inner aspects of affairs. However, this explanation is, in my view, open to question, because His saying afterward, ﴿and He is Knowing of everything﴾, would then be a repetition. But on the first explanation its placement is fitting, because the sense becomes as if it were said: no one encompasses Him or reaches His secrets, and nothing of the states of others is hidden from Him. Its parallel is: ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116].

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verses 4–6:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾. This has been explained in Surah al-A'raf, and the purpose of it is the signs of power.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it﴾. This has been explained in Surah Saba', and the purpose of it is the perfection of knowledge. He placed the attribute of power before the attribute of knowledge because knowledge that He, exalted is He, is Able comes before knowledge that He, exalted is He, is Knowing. For this reason a group of the muhaqqiqun (verifying scholars) held that the first knowledge of Allah is knowledge of Him as Able, while others held that the first knowledge of Allah is knowledge of Him as the Effecting Cause (mu'aththir). On both views, knowledge of Him as Able precedes knowledge of Him as Knowing.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are, and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that it is established that everything other than the Necessary True Being is contingent (mumkin), and every contingent thing's existence is from the Necessary Being. Therefore, the arrival of a contingent quiddity (mahiyyah) at its existence occurs through the Necessary True Being's bestowing that existence upon that quiddity. Thus the Real, glorified is He, is the intermediary between every quiddity and its existence; He is nearer to every quiddity than that quiddity's existence is. From this secret the muhaqqiqun said: "I have not seen anything except that I have seen Allah before it." The mutawassitun (intermediaries) said: "I have not seen anything except that I have seen Allah with it." And the zahiriyyun (literalists) said: "I have not seen anything except that I have seen Allah after it."

Know that these subtleties which we have made clear in these places have two levels. The first: that a person reaches them by means of reflection, deliberation, contemplation and pondering. The second level: that there arises in the person a taste-based power and an experiential state that cannot be expressed, and the relation of perception accompanied by taste to perception without taste is like the relation of one who eats sugar to one who describes its sweetness with his tongue.

The second issue: The mutakallimun said: this being-with (ma'iyyah) is either by knowledge or by protection and watchfulness. On either reading, there is consensus that He, glorified is He, is not with us in place, direction, or space. Therefore His saying, ﴿And He is with you﴾, necessarily requires interpretation (ta'wil), and if we permit interpretation in one place, it is required to permit it in all other places.

The third issue: Know that in these verses there is a remarkable order, for by His saying, ﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Manifest and the Hidden﴾ [al-Hadid: 3], He showed that He is the God of all possible and existent things. Then He showed that He is the God of the Throne, the heavens and the earths. Then He showed, by His saying, ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾, His being-with us through power, bringing into existence and originating, and through knowledge, which is His being Knowing of our outward and inward states. So reflect on how this order is arranged, then reflect on the wording of these verses, for in them are wondrous secrets and admonitions to lofty matters.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ (meaning: to the place where there is no owner other than Him). By this statement He indicated the affirmation of the Return (al-ma'ad).

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. The explanation of these verses has already been given in the other surahs. They combine the indication of His power with the manifestation of His blessings. The purpose of repeating them is to rouse one to reflection and contemplation, and then to occupy oneself with gratitude.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned kinds of evidence for His oneness, knowledge and power, He followed them with the obligations (al-takalif), and He began with the command to believe in Allah and His Messenger. If it is asked: Is His saying ﴿Believe﴾ addressed to one who already knows Allah, or to one who does not know Allah? If it is the first, then it is a command that he who knows should know, and this would be a command to obtain what is already obtained (tahsil al-hasil), which is impossible. If it is the second, then the address is directed to one who does not know Him, and one who does not know Him cannot know that he is commanded by this command; so the command would be directed to one who cannot know that he is obligated by it, and this is the imposition of what cannot be borne (taklif ma la yutaq). The answer: Some people have said that knowledge of the existence of the Creator is attained by all, and the intended purpose of this command is knowledge of the attributes.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend of that which He has made you successors concerning it. So those among you who believe and spend, for them is a great reward﴾. In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that He first commanded people to occupy themselves with obedience to Allah, then secondly commanded them to abandon the world, turn away from it, and spend it in the way of Allah, as He said: ﴿Say: "Allah," then leave them﴾. So His saying ﴿Say: "Allah"﴾ is what is meant here by His saying ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾, and His saying ﴿then leave them﴾ [al-An'am: 91] is what is meant here by His saying ﴿and spend of that which He has made you successors concerning it﴾.

The second issue: The verse has two interpretations.

The first: The wealth that is in your hands is in reality the wealth of Allah, by His creating and originating it. Then He placed it under the control of the accountable person (al-mukallaf) and under his disposal, so that he may benefit from it in accordance with the permission of the Law. Thus the accountable person, in his disposal of this wealth, is in the position of an agent (wakil), a deputy (na'ib), and a successor (khalifah). It is therefore required that spending from that wealth be easy for you, just as spending from another's wealth is easy for a man when that person has permitted him to do so.

The second: He made you successors to those who were before you, because He transferred their wealth to you by way of inheritance. So take heed from their condition: just as it passed from them to you, it will pass from you to others, so do not be stingy with it.

The third issue: They differed concerning this spending. Some of them said: it is the obligatory zakat. Others said: rather, voluntary charity (tatawwu') is also included in it, and there is no impediment to its being general, encompassing all the forms of righteousness. Then He, exalted is He, guaranteed for the one who does this a great reward, saying:

صفحة ١٨٩
﴿So those among you who believe and spend, for them is a great reward﴾. The judge (al-Qadi) said: This verse indicates that this great reward is not attained by faith alone until this spending is joined to it. Thus, from this aspect, it indicates that whoever neglects an obligation, such as zakat or other than it, has no reward.

Know that this inference is weak, because the verse indicates that whoever neglects the obligatory zakat does not attain that great reward; so why do you say that it indicates that he has no reward at all?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not believe in Allah, while the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant, if you are [truly] believers?﴾.

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that He, exalted is He, rebuked them for not believing on two conditions. The first: that the Messenger calls them, meaning that he recites to them the Qur'an, which contains clear proofs. The second: that He took a covenant (mithaq) from them. The commentators have mentioned two views regarding the taking of the covenant:

The first: it refers to the proofs established in the intellects that necessitate accepting the call of the messengers. Know that just as those proofs require acceptance, they are more binding than an oath and a pledge, and therefore He called it a covenant (mithaq). The essential point is that the proofs of transmission (naql) and reason ('aql) agree. As for transmission, it is by His saying: ﴿while the Messenger calls you﴾; as for reason, it is by His saying: ﴿and He has already taken your covenant﴾. When these two kinds come together, the matter has reached a point where nothing more can be added to it. Whoever claims that the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, is obligatory only through revelation (al-sam') has used this verse as evidence. He said: Because He, exalted is He, blamed them on the basis that the Messenger calls them, so we know that deserving blame arises only when the Messenger calls.

The second view regarding the interpretation of the taking of the covenant: 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: it refers to the time when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam, and He said: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. This view is weak, because He mentioned the taking of the covenant so that it would be a cause for them having no excuse for not believing after that. The taking of the covenant at the time of their being brought forth from the loins of Adam is not known to the people except through the word of the Messenger. Thus, before knowing the truthfulness of the Messenger, that would not be a cause for the obligation of believing the Messenger. As for the establishing of the proofs and clear signs, it is known to everyone, so that is a cause for the obligation of believing in the Messenger. Thus we know that interpreting the verse in this sense is not permissible.

The second issue: The Qadi (al-Qadi) said: His saying ﴿And what is [wrong] with you﴾ indicates their capability to believe, since such a statement may only be made to one who is able to perform the act, just as one does not say: "What is [wrong] with you that you do not grow tall or become white?" This indicates that capability (istita'ah) precedes the act, that power (qudrah) is suitable for both opposites, and that belief occurs through the servant and not through the creation of Allah.

The third issue: It was read: "and He has already taken your covenant" with the verb in the active voice. As for His saying ﴿if you are [truly] believers﴾, the meaning is: if you believe in something on account of a proof, then what is [wrong] with you that you do not believe now, since the transmitted and rational proofs have agreed and have reached a level beyond which no addition is possible.

[p. 190]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sends down upon His servant clear signs, that He may bring you out of darknesses into light. Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to you.﴾

Al-Qadi said: By this He explained that His purpose in sending down the clear signs, which are the Qur'an and other miracles, is to bring them out of darknesses into light. He reinforced this with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to you.﴾ Had He intended for some of them to remain in the darkness of disbelief, and created that in them, and decreed it for them with a decree that does not accept removal, this statement would not be valid. If it is said: Does not its apparent meaning indicate that He brings them out of darknesses into light, so that faith must be from His action? We say: If He intended by this bringing-out the creation of faith in them, then His saying ﴿It is He who sends down upon His servant clear signs, that He may bring you out﴾ would have no meaning, because whether that was preceded or not, His creating it for what He created does not change. Therefore the meaning is that He is gracious to them in bringing them out of darknesses into light, and were it not so, it would not be more appropriate for Him to describe Himself as bringing them out of darknesses into light than to describe Himself as bringing them out of light into darknesses.

Know that this statement, despite its baseness and evasiveness, is refuted by knowledge. That is because He, exalted is He, knew that His knowledge of their non-faith was established, and knew that this knowledge contradicts the existence of faith. So when He obligates them to bring about one of two opposites, while He knows that the other opposite exists in actuality in a way that it is not possible to remove or nullify it, would it be conceivable, along with that, that He intends by that good and benevolence for them? There is no doubt that this is something no rational person would say. And when the refutation is directed at it, that force disappears. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to you﴾, some have taken it to refer only to the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), and this restriction has no basis. Rather, it includes that together with all else by which a person is enabled to fulfill the obligations.

﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah, when to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth? Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah, when to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth?﴾

When He first commanded faith and spending, then in the previous verse emphasized the obligation of faith, He followed it in this verse by emphasizing the obligation of spending. The meaning is: you will die and be inherited, so why not put it forward in spending in obedience to Allah? Its verification is that wealth must leave the hand, either by death or by spending in the way of Allah. If it occurs in the first way, its effect is curse, abhorrence, and punishment; and if it occurs in the second way, its effect is praise and reward. And since it must leave the hand, every rational person knows that its leaving the hand in a manner that results in praise and reward is better than its leaving in a manner that results in curse and punishment.

Then, when He, exalted is He, explained that spending is a virtue, He explained that competing in spending is the completion of virtue, so He said:

﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought.﴾ Concerning this there are issues:

The first issue: the estimated sense of the verse is: not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and those who spent after the conquest, as He said: ﴿Not equal are the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise﴾ [al-Hashr: 20], except that it was omitted for the clarity of the situation.

The second issue: by this conquest is meant the conquest of Mecca, because the word "conquest" in common usage refers to it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no migration after the conquest." Abu Muslim said: The Qur'an indicates another conquest by His saying: ﴿So He made after that a near conquest﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. Whichever it is, Allah has explained the great standing of spending before the conquest.

The third issue: al-Kalbi said: This verse was revealed concerning the virtue of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, because he was the first to spend wealth on the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the way of Allah. Umar said: "I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and with him was Abu Bakr, wearing a cloak which he had fastened at his chest with a skewer. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended and said: 'What is [the matter] with me that I see Abu Bakr wearing a cloak which he has fastened at his chest?' He said: 'He spent his wealth on me before the conquest.'"

Know that the verse indicates that whoever spends in the way of Allah and fights the enemies of Allah before the conquest is in a greater state than one from whom these two things come after the conquest. It is known that the one who spent is Abu Bakr, and the one who fought is Ali. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the one who spent before the one who fought, and in this there is an indication of giving precedence to Abu Bakr. Also, spending is from the category of mercy, and fighting is from the category of wrath, and He, exalted is He, said: "My mercy precedes My wrath," so precedence belongs to the one who spent. If it is said: Rather, the one who spent is Ali, due to His saying: ﴿and they feed the food﴾ [al-Insan: 8]. We say: The unrestricted statement that he spent is not realized except if he spent great wealth in great events. Al-Wahidi mentioned in al-Basit that Abu Bakr was the first to fight for Islam. Also, Ali at the beginning of the emergence of Islam was a small child and was not the one who fought. As for Abu Bakr, he was an honored elder, and he defended Islam until he was struck on its account with a blow that brought him near to death.

The fourth issue: the scholars of tawhid (theology) took this verse to indicate the virtue of those who preceded to Islam and spent and struggled alongside the Messenger (ﷺ) before the conquest. They explained the reason for this, which is the great standing of supporting the Messenger (peace be upon him) with oneself and spending wealth in that situation, when the Muslims were few in number and the disbelievers had strength and great numbers. So the need for support and assistance was greater, unlike what came after the conquest, for Islam had by then become strong and disbelief weak. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 100], and by the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Do not revile my companions. Were one of you to spend the like of Uhud in gold, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it."

[Page 192]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to each (of them) Allah has promised the best (reward), and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: That is, each one of the two groups, ﴿Allah has promised the best (reward)﴾, meaning the best recompense, which is Paradise, with differences in ranks.

The second issue: The well-known reading is ﴿wa-kullan﴾ with the accusative (naṣb), because it is like the sentence "Zaydan, I promised him good," so it is the object of waʿada (promised). Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿wa-kullun﴾ with the nominative (rafʿ). His argument is that when the verb is placed after its object, its action does not take effect on it. The evidence for this is that they say: "Zaydun ḍarabtu" (Zayd, I struck), and as in his saying in poetry:

*Qad aṣbaḥat Umm al-Khiyār tadaʿʿī*
*ʿalayya dhanban kulluhu lam aṣniʿ*

(Umm al-Khiyar has come to claim against me a sin, all of it, which I did not commit.)

It is narrated as "kulluhu" with the nominative, because the verb is placed after it for another reason. Know that Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qāhir has a fine discussion on this topic. He said: The meaning in this verse varies according to the accusative and the nominative. The accusative indicates that he did not do all the sins, and this does not contradict his having done some of the sins. For when he says, "I did not do all the sins," it means that he did not do the whole, and there remains the possibility that he did some of them. Indeed, according to the one who holds that *dalīl al-khiṭāb* (the argument from implication, i.e. inferring the opposite meaning from a restricted statement) is a valid proof, that would be an acknowledgement that he did some of the sins. As for the nominative narration, which is his saying "kulluhu lam aṣniʿ," its meaning is that each one of the sins is judged to be not done, so its meaning is that he did not commit any of the sins at all. The poet's purpose is to claim innocence from all the sins. So we know that the meaning varies with the nominative and the accusative. Among the cases in which the meaning varies because of variation in *iʿrāb* (grammatical case inflection) in this topic is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49]. Whoever reads "kulla shayʾin" with the accusative means that Allah created all things by a measure. Whoever reads "kullu" with the nominative does not mean that Allah created all things, but rather means that whatever was created by Him, He created it by a measure. Sometimes the variation in *iʿrāb* in this topic does not cause a variation in meaning, as in His saying: ﴿And the moon—We have measured it﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 39]. For whether you read "wa-l-qamaru" with the nominative or the accusative, the meaning is one. Likewise in this verse: whether you read ﴿wa-kullan waʿada Allāhu al-ḥusnā﴾ or read "wa-kullun waʿada Allāhu al-ḥusnā," the meaning is one and does not vary.

The third issue: The implied construction of the verse is: "And to each of them Allah has promised the best," except that the pronoun was omitted because it is evident, as in His saying: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 41], and likewise His saying: ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ The meaning is that when He promised the foremost and the good-doers the reward, He must necessarily have knowledge of the particulars and of all that is known, so that He is able to deliver the reward to those who deserve it. For if He did not have knowledge of them and of their actions in detail, it would not be possible to fully discharge the obligation of the promise. For this reason, He followed that promise with His saying: ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan?﴾

Concerning this, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** They mention that "when this verse was revealed, a man from the Jews said: 'The god of Muhammad has become needy and asks us for loans.' Abu Bakr slapped him, so the Jew complained of this to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said to him: 'What did you intend by that?' He said: 'I could not restrain myself from slapping him.' Then there was revealed His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associate others with God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 186]." The scholars who investigate said: the Jew said that only as mockery, not because a sensible person believes that God becomes needy. The same applies to their saying: ﴿Indeed, God is poor and we are rich﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181].

**The second issue:** By this verse, He emphasized encouraging people to spend their wealth in support of the Muslims, in fighting the disbelievers, and in aiding the poor among the Muslims. He called that spending a "loan" because He promised Paradise for it, by way of comparison with a loan.

**The third issue:** They differed about what this spending refers to. Some said it means the obligatory expenditures, while others said it refers to voluntary charities. The more correct view is that it includes all of them.

**The fourth issue:** They mentioned several aspects regarding the loan being "goodly":

The first: Muqatil said: it means that the soul is content with it (lit. "good in it").

The second: al-Kalbi said: it means one gives it in charity for the sake of God.

The third: some scholars said: a loan is not goodly until it combines ten attributes:

The first: that it be from what is lawful. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «Indeed God is Good and accepts only what is good.» And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «God does not accept a prayer without purification, nor charity from ill-gotten gains (ghulul).»

The second: that it be of the best of what one owns, not giving the inferior. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not aim at the bad [part] of it to spend from it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 267].

The third: that you give it while you love it and need it, by hoping for life. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and gives wealth in spite of love for it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 177], and His saying: ﴿and they give food in spite of love for it﴾ [Al-Insan: 8], according to one of the interpretations. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Charity is that you give while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for prosperity, and do not delay until, when you reach the collarbones, you say: 'To so-and-so such-and-such, and to so-and-so such-and-such.'"

The fourth: that you direct your charity to the most needy who is most deserving of taking it; for this reason God specified certain groups for receiving it, namely the people entitled to the shares (ahl al-sihan).

The fifth: that you conceal the charity as much as you can, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 271].

The sixth: that you do not follow it with reminders or injury. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 264].

The seventh: that you intend by it the face of God and do not show off, as He said: ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High, and he will surely be satisfied﴾ [Al-Layl: 20–21], and because the one who shows off is blameworthy by consensus.

The eighth: that you consider what you give to be small, even if it is great, because it is a small part of this world, and the world entire is small. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not bestow favor seeking to receive more﴾ [Al-Muddaththir: 6], according to one of the interpretations.

The ninth: that it be from your most beloved wealth, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 92].

The tenth: that you do not see your own honor and the poor man's humiliation, but rather the matter be reversed in your view, so that you see the poor man as if God, exalted is He, had assigned to you his provision, which He guaranteed by His saying: ﴿There is no creature on earth but that upon God is its provision﴾ [Hud: 6], and you see yourself as being in debt to the poor man. These are ten attributes; when they come together, the charity becomes a goodly loan. This verse is explained in Surat al-Baqarah.

* *

Then, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿so He will multiply it for him, and he will have a noble reward﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** For this goodly loan, He, exalted is He, guaranteed two things:

One of them: the multiplication, as mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, and He made clear that along with the multiplication there is for him a noble reward. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: this is the view of our companions (the Ash'arites) that the multiplication indicates that He adds to the measure of the reward an equal amount as a bounty. The "noble reward" is an expression for the reward. If it is said: "Your doctrine is that the reward is also a bounty, so if no distinction is achieved, this explanation is not complete." The answer: God wrote in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) that whoever performs such-and-such an act will have such-and-such an amount of reward. That amount is the reward, and when an equal amount is added to it, that equal amount is the doubling.

The second view: this is the view of al-Jubba'i (the Mu'tazilite theologian) that the compensations (a'wad) are added to the reward, and that is the multiplication. He described the reward as "noble" only because it is what brought about that doubling, and through it that increase was obtained, so it is noble from this standpoint.

**The second issue:** Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿fa-yudha''ifahu﴾ with a doubled ḍād and without an alif, and Ibn Kathir recited it with a ḍammah on the fā', while Ibn 'Amir recited it with a fatḥah on the fā'. 'Asim recited ﴿fa-yuḍā'ifahu﴾ with an alif and a fatḥah on the fā'. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿fa-yuḍā'ifuhu﴾ with an alif and a ḍammah on the fā'. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "yuḍā'afu" and "yuḍa''afu" have the same meaning. The real matter is in explaining the justification for the recitation in the nominative (raf') and the accusative (nasb). As for the nominative, its basis is clear, because it is coordinated with "yuqriḍu" (the verb of lending), or it is an independent resumption from the former, as if it were said: "so He multiplies it." As for the accusative recitation, its basis is that when He said: ﴿Who is it that will lend﴾, it is as if He had said: "Will anyone lend to God a goodly loan?" Then His saying ﴿so He will multiply it for him﴾ serves as an answer to that interrogation, and therefore it is put in the accusative.
