Then God Most High said: ﴿On the Day you will see the believing men and the believing women, their light running before them and on their right hands﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: ﴿On the Day you see﴾ is a time adverbial (ẓarf) governed by His saying: ﴿and theirs will be a generous reward﴾, or it is in the accusative governed by "remember" (udhkur), to glorify that Day.

The second issue: What is meant by this Day is the Day of Reckoning. The scholars differed concerning this light in several respects:

The first of them: Some said: What is meant is the light itself, as has been related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Every one who is rewarded will have a light according to the magnitude and the smallness of his deed and reward." According to this, the ranks of the lights vary. Among them is one for whom a light shines as far as between Aden and Sana'a; among them is one whose light is like a mountain; among them is one for whom a light shines only as far as the place of his feet; and the least in light is one whose light is on his big toe, which goes out at times and flares up at others. This view is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah and others. Mujahid said: "No servant will be left but that on the Day of Resurrection he will be called: O so-and-so, here is your light; and O so-and-so, you have no light. We seek refuge in God from that." Know that we have explained in the Surah of al-Nur that the true Light is God Most High, and that the light of knowledge, which is the light of insight, is more worthy of being called light than the light of sight. Since this is so, it becomes clear that the knowledge of God is the light on the Day of Resurrection, so the measures of the lights on the Day of Resurrection correspond to the measures of the knowledge in this world.

The second view: That what is meant by the light is that which becomes a cause of salvation. He said: ﴿before them and on their right hands﴾ because the blessed are given the records of their deeds from these two directions, just as the wretched are given them from their left sides and from behind their backs.

The third view: What is meant by this light is guidance to Paradise, as one says: "This matter has no light" when the intended goal is not attained, and one says: "This matter has light and radiance" when the intended goal is attained.

The third issue: Sahl ibn Shu'ayb read "wa-bi-imanihim" with a kasra on the hamza, and the meaning is: their light runs before them and by their faith that running has come about. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent before﴾ [al-Hajj: 10], meaning: that is occurring because of that.

* *
* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿Good news for you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: The reality of glad tidings (bishara) we have mentioned in the explanation of His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25]. Then they said: The implied sense of the verse is: and the angels will say to them: "Good news for you today," as He said: ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying]: Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23-24].

The second issue: This verse indicates that the believers will not be touched by the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, because He, exalted is He, made clear that this is their description on the Day of Resurrection without any restriction.

The third issue: al-Ka'bi argued that the sinner (fasiq) is not a believer, saying: If he were a believer he would enter under this glad tiding, and if that were so he would be certain that he is among the people of Paradise; since he is not certain, it is established that he is not a believer. The answer: The sinner is certain that he is among the people of Paradise, because either he will not enter the Fire, or if he enters it he will certainly come out of it and enter Paradise and remain there forever and ever. Thus he is certain that he is among the people of Paradise, and so this argument falls.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿That﴾ refers to everything mentioned before, namely the light and the glad tidings of the everlasting gardens.

The fifth issue: It has been read: "dhalika al-fawz," with the word "huwa" omitted.

Know that when God Most High had explained the condition of the believers at the standing place of the Resurrection, He followed this with an explanation of the condition of the hypocrites.

He said: ﴿On the Day the hypocritical men and the hypocritical women will say to those who believed: "Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light." It will be said: "Turn back behind you and seek a light"﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: "On the Day they will say" is a substitute for ﴿On the Day you see﴾, or it is likewise in the accusative governed by an implied "remember."

The second issue: Hamza alone read "unzirna" with a kasra on the ẓa', and the rest read "unzuru". Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The word naẓar (looking) is used in several ways:

The first: that you mean by it "I looked at the thing," so the preposition is dropped and the verb is connected directly, as Abu al-Hasan recited:
"Beautiful and graceful, they look as the gazelles look at the arak trees"
The meaning is: they look at the arak trees.
The second: that you mean by it "I considered and reflected," and from it is your saying: "Go and look at Zayd, does he believe?" This is meant as consideration, and from it is His saying: ﴿Look how they have struck for you the parables﴾ [al-Isra: 48], ﴿Look how they fabricate lies against God﴾ [al-Nisa: 50], ﴿Look how We have preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Isra: 21]. He said: It may also be followed by "ila," as in His saying: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17], and this is explicit about consideration, and the wisdom in it is clear. It may also be followed by "fi," as in His saying: ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ and ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾
The third: that by looking is meant seeing, as in the verse:
"When Hawran appeared and the mirage lay before it, you looked but you did not look with your eye at a sight"
The meaning is: you looked, but you did not see with your eye a sight that you recognized in the mirage. He said: However, this is in the manner of metaphor (majaz), because the evidences show that looking is an expression for the turning of the pupil toward the seen object seeking to see it; and since seeing is generally a consequence and concomitant of looking, the word "looking" was applied to seeing by way of naming the cause for the effect. He said: It is also possible that his saying "you looked and did not look" is like the saying "you spoke and did not speak," meaning you did not speak words of benefit; so here too: you looked, and did not look a beneficial look.
The fourth: that looking means waiting, and from it is His saying: ﴿to food, not waiting for its preparation﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], meaning not waiting for its ripening and readiness. On this view, "nazartu" means "intazartu" (I waited). The coming of fa'ala and if'tala with one meaning is common, as in the saying: "shawaytu" and "ashtawaytu," "haqartu" and "ihtaqartu," when you know this, then His saying: ﴿unzurūna﴾ may bear two meanings:

The first: "unzurūna," that is, "intazirūna" (wait for us), because the believers are hastened to Paradise like flashing lightnings, while the hypocrites are on foot.

The second: "unzurūna," that is, "unzurū ilaynā" (look at us), because when they look at them they face them with their faces, and the light is before them, so they are illuminated by it. As for the reading "unzirna" with a kasra on the ẓa', it is from respite and reprieve, and from it is His saying: ﴿Reprieve me until the day they are raised﴾ [al-A'raf: 14], and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded giving respite to the debtor in difficulty. The meaning is that they made their walking slow until they would catch up with them, granting them a respite.

Know that Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash used to criticize the soundness of this reading, and the manner of its soundness has now become clear.

The third issue: Know that the possibilities in this matter are three:

The first: that all people are in darkness, then God, exalted is He, gives these lights to the believers, and the hypocrites ask them for them.

The second: that all people are in the lights, then the believers will be in the gardens and pass quickly, while the hypocrites remain behind them and ask them to wait.

The third: that the believers are in the light and the hypocrites are in darkness, then the hypocrites ask the believers for the light. Some have gone to each one of these possibilities. If this condition occurs at the standing place, then what is meant by His saying "unzurūna" is "look at us," because when they look at them they have turned toward them, and whenever they turn toward them while their lights are in front of them, they are illuminated by those lights. If this condition occurs at the believers' journey to Paradise, then what is meant by His saying "unzurūna" may be waiting, and it may be looking at them.

The fourth issue: The qabas is a flame of fire or of a lamp. The hypocrites hoped to take some of the lights of the believers as one borrows the fires of this world, and this is ignorance on their part, because those lights are the fruits of righteous deeds in this world; when those deeds were not found in this world, the attainment of those lights in the Hereafter was impossible. Al-Hasan said: On the Day of Resurrection each person is given a light according to the measure of his deed; then it is taken from the heat of Hell and from what is in it of hooks and thorns, and it is cast upon the path. A group of believers passes with faces like the moon on the night of the full moon; then another group passes like the lights of the stars in the sky; then after that a darkness covers them and extinguishes the light of the hypocrites. At that moment the hypocrites say to the believers: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾, like the borrowing of a fire.

The fifth issue: They have mentioned several meanings for the saying of God Most High: ﴿It will be said: "Turn back behind you and seek a light"﴾:

The first: that what is meant by it is: return to the abode of the world and seek these lights there, for these lights are only produced by acquiring divine knowledge, noble character, and purification from ignorance and blameworthy traits. And what is meant by the striking of the wall (al-sur) is the prevention of returning to the world.

The second: Abu Umama said: People will be in intense darkness, then the believers will be given lights, so when the believer hastens onward, the hypocrite says: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾, and it will be said to them: ﴿Turn back behind you and seek a light﴾. He said: This is a deception by which the hypocrites were deceived, as He said: ﴿They deceive God, but He is their Deceiver﴾ [al-Nisa: 142]. So they return to the place where the light was divided, and find nothing; then they turn back to the believers and find the wall struck between them and the believers.

The third: Abu Muslim said: What is meant by the believers' saying "Turn back" is preventing the hypocrites from being illuminated, like a man's saying to one who wants to come near him: "Behind you, I will make room for you." According to this view, what is intended by His saying "Turn back" is that they should be certain there is no way for them to obtain this sought thing at all, not that it is a command to them to return.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verse 13:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So a wall will be set up between them, with a gate; its inner side will have mercy, and its outer side will have torment before it.﴾ In it are two issues:

The first issue: They differed concerning the sur (wall). Some said: what is meant by it is a screen and a barrier, that is, the hypocrites were prevented from pursuing the believers. Others said: rather, what is meant is a wall between Paradise and Hell; this is the view of Qatada. Mujahid said: it is the screen of al-A'raf.

The second issue: The ba' (the particle "bi") in His saying ﴿bi-sur﴾ is a ṣila (an extra connecting particle) and it is for emphasis (li-al-ta'kid), and the implied sense is: "a wall such-and-such was set up between them." This was said by al-Akhfash. Then He said ﴿lahu bab﴾, that is, that wall has a gate, ﴿whose inner side has mercy in it﴾, that is, in the inner part of that wall is mercy, and by mercy is meant Paradise, in which the believers are. ﴿And its outer side﴾, meaning outside the wall, ﴿from before it is torment﴾, that is, from its direction torment comes to them. The meaning is that what is adjacent to the believers has mercy in it, and from the direction of what is adjacent to the disbelievers, torment comes to them. The upshot is that between Paradise and Hell there is a wall, and that wall has a gate. So the believers enter Paradise through the gate of that wall, while the disbelievers remain in torment and in the Fire.

Then the verse: ﴿They will call out to them: "Were we not with you?" They will say: "Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, and you waited, and you doubted, and false hopes deluded you until the command of Allah came."﴾

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will call out to them, "Were we not with you?" They will say, "Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, waited, doubted, and were deceived by false hopes until the command of Allah came."﴾ On this verse there are two issues.

The first issue: concerning the verse there are two opinions.

The first: ﴿Were we not with you?﴾ refers to the worldly life.

The second: ﴿Were we not with you?﴾ refers to acts of worship, the mosques, the prayers, and the military campaigns, and this is the opinion that is definite (al-mutaʿayyin).

The second issue: The distance between Paradise and Hell is great, since Paradise is in the highest heavens while Hell is in the lowest abyss (al-darak al-asfal). This shows that great distance does not prevent hearing (al-idrak). It cannot be said that Allah magnified the voice of the disbelievers so that it reaches from the lowest of the lowest to the highest of the 'Illiyyun, because such a voice befits only the very strong and powerful, whereas the disbelievers are described as weak and having faint voices. So we know that distance does not prevent perception, according to our school of thought. Then Allah the Exalted related that the believers said: "Yes, you were with us, but you did things because of which you fell into this punishment."

The first of these is: ﴿but you led yourselves into temptation﴾, that is, through disbelief and sins, and all of them are temptation (fitnah).

The second is His saying: ﴿and waited﴾, and concerning it there are several views:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "You waited for repentance."

The second: Muqatil said: "And you waited for Muhammad's death; you said, 'He is about to die, so we will be relieved of him.'"

The third: You were waiting for the calamity of misfortune (daʾirat al-suʾ) to befall the believers, so that you could join the disbelievers and be freed from hypocrisy.

The third: His saying: ﴿and doubted﴾, and concerning it there are several views:

The first: You doubted the threat (waʿid) of Allah.

The second: You doubted the prophethood of Muhammad.

The third: You doubted the resurrection and the Day of Judgment.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿and were deceived by false hopes﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means falsehood, namely what they used to wish for regarding the misfortunes descending upon the believers. ﴿until the command of Allah came﴾, meaning death. The meaning is: they remained in the deceptions and delusions of Satan until Allah caused them to die and cast them into the Fire.

**Verse 15: "And the Deceiver deceived you concerning Allah."**

Its discussion has two issues.

**First issue:** Simak ibn Harb recited *al-ghurūr* (الغُرُورُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *ghayn*. The meaning is "and *al-ightirār* (the state of being deceived) deceived you concerning Allah." Its construction, with an elided genitive (*al-muḍāf*, "the thing that is added"), is: "your being safe from Him, together with your being deceived, deceived you concerning Allah."

**Second issue:** *al-Gharūr* with a *fatḥa* on the *ghayn* is Satan, because he casts into you that there is no fear for you of reckoning and recompense.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: **"So today no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved."**

*Al-fidyah* (ransom) is that by which one ransoms oneself. There are two views on it:

The first: no faith and no repentance will be taken from you, for the obligation has ended and compulsion has taken place.

The second: rather, the meaning is that no ransom by which you would ward off punishment from yourselves will be accepted from you, like His statement: **"nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it"** [al-Baqarah: 123]. Know that *al-fidyah* is that by which one ransoms oneself, so it includes faith, repentance and wealth. This indicates that accepting repentance is not obligatory by reason, according to what the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) say, because He, exalted, has made clear that He does not accept any ransom at all, and repentance is a ransom. So the verse indicates that repentance is not accepted at all, and if that is so, accepting repentance is not obligatory by reason.

As for His statement, **"nor from those who disbelieved,"** there is a question (*baḥth*) here: conjoining the disbeliever to the hypocrite requires that the hypocrite not be a disbeliever, since the conjoined and the conjoined-to must be different. (The answer): the intended meaning is those who openly showed disbelief; otherwise the hypocrite is a disbeliever.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: **"Your refuge is the Fire; it is your protector (*mawlākum*), and wretched is the destination."**

Regarding the word *mawlā* here, there are several views:

First: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "*Mawlākum*" means "your destination." Its realization is that *al-mawlā* is the place of *al-waly*, which is nearness. So the meaning is that the Fire is the place you draw near to and arrive at.

Second: al-Kalbi said: it means "more deserving of you." This is the view of al-Zajjaj, al-Farra' and Abu ʿUbaydah. Know that what they said is a meaning, not an explanation of the word. For if *mawlā* and *awlā* (more deserving) had one meaning in the language, then each of them would be valid in the place of the other. It would then be correct to say "this is *mawlā* of so-and-so" as one says "this is *awlā* than so-and-so," and correct to say "this is *awlā* of so-and-so" as one says "this is *mawlā* of so-and-so." Since this is invalid, we know that what they said is a meaning and not an explanation. We have pointed out this subtle matter because al-Sharif al-Murtada, when he relied on the imamate of ʿAli by the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: **"Whoever I am his *mawlā*, then ʿAli is his *mawlā*,"** said that one of the meanings of *mawlā* is that he is *awlā* (more deserving). He argued for this with the views of the linguistic authorities in explaining this verse, that *mawlā* means *awlā*. Once it is established that the word admits this meaning, it must be taken to it, because whatever else it could mean is either certainly established, like being a cousin or a helper, or certainly negated, like a manumitter and the one manumitted. On the first assumption it would be pointless, and on the second it would be false. As for us, we have shown by evidence that their view in this place is a meaning and not an explanation, and then the argument based on it falls away.

There is another possibility in the verse: the meaning of His statement **"it is your *mawlā*"** is: you have no *mawlā*. This is because whoever has the Fire as his *mawlā* has no *mawlā*, just as one says: his helper is abandonment and his aid is weeping, meaning he has no helper and no aid. This interpretation is reinforced by His statement, exalted: **"and that the disbelievers have no protector (*mawlā*)"** [Muḥammad: 11]. And from it is His statement: **"they will be given water like molten brass"** [al-Kahf: 29].

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verse 16:**

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah and to what has been revealed of the truth, and that they should not be like those who were given the Scripture before, and the term grew long for them, so their hearts became hardened? And many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

Under this verse there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Hasan recited: ﴿ألَمّا يَأْنِ﴾ (alamma ya'ni). Ibn Jinni said: the origin of *lamma* (لَمّا) is *lam* (لَمْ), to which *ma* (ما) was added. So *lam* is the negation of the verbal form "af'alu" (I do), while *lamma* is the negation of "qad yaf'alu" (he has [perhaps] done). This is because when *qad* was added to the affirmative, it was necessary to add *ma* to its negation. However, when they combined *lam* with *ma*, the combination acquired a meaning and a form. As for the meaning, in some contexts it became a temporal adverb (*zarf*), as in: *lamma qumta qama Zaydun*, meaning "at the time of your standing, Zayd stood." As for the form, it is permissible to pause on it without its jussive complement, so one may say: *ji'tu wa-lamma* (I came, and not yet [he came]), meaning *wa-lamma yajii'* (and he has not yet come), but it is not permissible to say: *ji'tu wa-lam* (I came, and not [he came]).

As for those who recited: ﴿ألَمْ يَأْنِ﴾ (alam ya'ni), the well-known reading is *alam ya'ni*, from *anā al-amr yaʼnī* (the matter came, "anā"), meaning when it came to its proper time (*innahu*, i.e., its time). It was also read: *alam ya'in*, from *ann yaʼīnu*, with the same meaning as *anā yaʼnī*.

The second issue: The scholars differed concerning the words of Allah: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah﴾. Some said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites who displayed faith while hypocrisy, which is incompatible with humility, was in their hearts. Those who hold this view apparently went on the basis that a believer is not truly a believer except with humility of heart, so Allah would not say this except to one who is not a believer. Others said: Rather, the intended people are those who are truly believers, but a believer may or may not have humility and fear. On this view, the verse admits several interpretations:

First: Perhaps a group of believers did not have an abundance of humility or tenderness, so they were urged toward it by this verse.

Second: Perhaps a people had great humility, then the intensity of that humility departed from them, so they were urged to return to it. It is narrated from al-A'mash, who said: When the Companions came to Madinah, they found ease and comfort in livelihood, so they slackened in some of what they had been upon, and they were reproached by this verse. And it is narrated from Abu Bakr that this verse was recited in his presence, and with him was a people from the people of al-Yamama, who wept intensely. He looked at them and said: "This is how we were, until the hearts hardened."

As for His words: ﴿for the remembrance of Allah﴾, there are two views:

The first: The sense of the verse is: "Has it not come time for the believers that their hearts should be softened by the remembrance of Allah," meaning the admonitions of Allah which He mentioned in the Qur'an. On this view, *dhikr* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) annexed to its agent.

The second view: *Dhikr* is annexed to its object, and the meaning is: "for their remembrance of Allah," i.e., the remembrance must bring about humility in them, and they should not be like one whose remembrance is in heedlessness, so his heart does not humble itself to the remembrance.

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿and what has been revealed of the truth﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: *ma* (ما) is in the genitive position by conjunction with *dhikr*, and it is a relative pronoun, its returning pronoun being omitted, according to the estimate: "and what has been revealed of the truth." Then Ibn Abbas said concerning His words ﴿and what has been revealed of the truth﴾: it means the Qur'an.

The second issue: Abu Ali said: Nafi', Hafs, and al-Mufaddal from Asim recited ﴿وما نَزَلَ مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾ with a light (unstressed) *nun*. The others, and Abu Bakr from Asim, recited *wa-ma nazzala* with a doubled *zay*. And from Abu Amr: *wa-ma nuzzila min al-haqq* with a raised *nun* and a kasra on the *zay*. The estimate in the first reading is: "that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah and to what has been revealed of the truth." In the second reading: "and to what Allah has sent down of the truth." In the third reading: "and to what has been sent down of the truth."

The third issue: It is possible that the intended "truth" is the Qur'an, because it combines both attributes: the remembrance and the admonition, and that it is a truth sent down from heaven. It is also possible that the intended "remembrance" is the remembrance of Allah in general, and what "has been revealed of the truth" is the Qur'an. The humility through the remembrance was placed before the humility through what was revealed of the Qur'an, because humility, fear, and awe arise only at the remembrance of Allah. As for their arising upon hearing the Qur'an, that is because the Qur'an includes the remembrance of Allah.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and that they should not be﴾. Al-Farra' said: It is in a place of accusative (*nasb*), its meaning being: "Has the time not come for their hearts to humble themselves, and that they should not be..." He said: If it were jussive by way of prohibition, it would be correct. This interpretation is supported by the reading of one who recited with a *ta'* (you), by way of *iltifat* (shift in address).

Then He said: ﴿like those who were given the Scripture before﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians. ﴿And the term grew long for them﴾. On this there are two issues:

The first issue: They mentioned several interpretations of the lengthening of the term:

First: The period between them and their prophets lengthened, so their hearts hardened.

Second: Ibn Abbas said: They inclined to the world and turned away from the admonitions of Allah.

Third: Their lifetimes lengthened in heedlessness, so hardness arose in their hearts for that reason.

Fourth: Ibn Hibban said: *al-amad* here means the far-reaching hope, and the meaning in this case is: "the term grew long for them through the length of hope," i.e., since their hopes lengthened, their hearts inevitably hardened.

Fifth: Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: the period of the Prophet's (ﷺ) emergence grew long for them.

Sixth: The time since they had heard the Torah and the Gospel lengthened, so their impact faded from their hearts, and therefore their hearts hardened. It is as if Allah forbade the believers from being like that. This was said by al-Qurazi.

The second issue: It has been read: *al-amadd* with a doubled *dal*, meaning the longest period.

Then He said: ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, i.e., they departed from their religion and rejected what was in the two Scriptures. It seems to be an indication that the absence of humility at the beginning of the matter leads to disobedience at its end.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Know that God gives life to the earth after its death. We have indeed made the signs clear to you, so that you may understand.﴾ On this verse there are two interpretations.

The first: it is a parable. The meaning is that hearts which have died through hardness, constant remembrance of God is a cause for the life of humility to return to them, just as God gives life to the earth through rain.

The second: what is meant by His words ﴿He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ is the resurrection of the dead. He mentions this to encourage humility and submission and to warn against hardness.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who lend to God a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a generous reward.﴾ On this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: Ibn Kathīr and ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abū Bakr, read (إنَّ المُصَدِّقِينَ والمُصَدِّقاتِ) with a light pronunciation (without the shadda on the ṣād). The rest, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, read ﴿إنَّ المُصَّدِّقِينَ والمُصَّدِّقاتِ﴾ with the ṣād doubled in both. According to the first reading, the meaning of al-muṣaddiq (the one who gives in charity) is the believer, so the meaning becomes ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 277], because lending to God is among the righteous deeds. Then they said: this reading is preferable for two reasons.

The first: whoever gives charity for God's sake and lends, if he is not a believer, does not enter under the promise. So on the doubled reading the apparent sense of the verse is left as it is, while on the light reading it is not left as it is.

The second: the one who gives charity is the one who lends to God, so His words ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity﴾ and His words ﴿and who lend to God﴾ become one thing, and this is repetition. On the light reading, repetition does not arise. The argument of those who transmitted the other reading has two points:

The first: in the reading of Ubayy: (والمُتَصَدِّقِينَ والمُتَصَدِّقاتِ) with a *tā'* (تَ).

The second: His words ﴿and who lend to God a goodly loan﴾ are a parenthetical insertion between the predicate and the subject it describes, and a parenthetical insertion has the function of a qualifier. So it is more closely bound to giving charity than to giving in charity (the verb of belief). Those who held the first view replied: we do not take His words ﴿and who lend﴾ as a parenthetical insertion, but we take it as coordinated with the meaning. Do you not see that the phrase (al-muṣaddiqīna wal-muṣaddiqāt) means: "those who gave in charity," so the sense of the verse becomes: "Indeed, those who gave in charity and lent to God."

The second issue: there is a difficulty in the verse, namely that coordinating a verb with a noun is ugly, so what is the benefit of adopting it here? The author of al-Kashshāf said: His words ﴿and who lend﴾ are coordinated with the meaning of the verb in (al-muṣaddiqīn), because the *lām* (ال) has the sense of "those who," and the active participle has the sense of "they gave in charity," as if it were said: "Indeed, those who gave in charity and lent." Know that this does not remove the difficulty, for it does not explain why the speech departed from that wording to this wording. What I think about it is that the *alif* and *lām* in (al-muṣaddiqīna wal-muṣaddiqāt) are for the known (the specific, previously known group), so it is as if He mentioned a group specified by this description. Then, before mentioning the predicate, He informed about them that they came with the best kind of charity, which is bringing the goodly loan. Then He mentioned the predicate after that, which is His words ﴿it will be multiplied for them﴾. So His words ﴿and who lend to God﴾ is what is called *ḥashw al-lawzanj* (a filler phrase, lit. "almond filling," a phrase inserted for embellishment), as in the poet's words:

"Indeed, eighty, and having reached it,
has made my hearing need an interpreter."

The third issue: whoever reads (al-muṣaddiqīn) with the doubled ṣād, the scholars differ as to whether what is meant is obligatory charity, voluntary charity, or both together. Or it is said that what is meant by giving charity is obligatory charity, and by lending is voluntary charity, since calling it a loan is like an indication of this. So all these possibilities are mentioned. As for His words ﴿it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a generous reward﴾, what has been said about it has already been presented.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and His messengers, they are the truthful (al-siddiqun) and the martyrs (al-shuhada') with their Lord. For them is their reward and their light. But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the blazing fire.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned before this verse the condition of the believers and the hypocrites, and now He mentions the condition of the believers and the disbelievers. Then, in the verse, there are two issues:

The first issue: al-siddiq (the truthful) is a description of one who speaks truth often and combines truth with truth in belief in Allah, exalted is He, and His messengers. Regarding this verse there are two opinions:

The first: the verse is general, applying to everyone who believes in Allah and His messengers. This is the view of Mujahid, who said: "Everyone who believes in Allah and His messengers is a siddiq," and then he recited this verse. What supports this is what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿they are the truthful﴾, meaning the monotheists (al-muwahhidun).

The second: the verse is specific. This is the saying of al-Muqatilun: the siddiqun are those who believed in the messengers when they came to them and never denied them even for an hour, such as the people of Yasin, and such as the believer of the family of Pharaoh. As for in our religion, they are eight who preceded the people of the earth to Islam: Abu Bakr, 'Ali, Zayd, 'Uthman, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd, Hamzah, and the ninth of them is 'Umar, whom Allah joined with them because of what He knew of the sincerity of his intention.

The second issue: regarding His saying: ﴿and the martyrs﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: it is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the previous verse, and the meaning is: Indeed those who believe in Allah and His messengers are the truthful and they are the martyrs. Mujahid said: "Every believer is a siddiq and a shahid," and he recited this verse. Regarding this view, they differed about why every believer is called a shahid. Some said: because believers are the witnesses before their Lord over the servants in their deeds, and what is meant is that they are the just ones of the Hereafter whose testimony is accepted. Al-Hasan said: the reason for this name is that every believer witnesses the honour of his Lord. Al-Asamm said: every believer is a shahid, because he stands before Allah, exalted is He, with testimony regarding what He has obligated upon them of the obligation of faith, the obligation of acts of obedience, and the prohibition of disbelief and sins. Abu Muslim said: We have mentioned that al-siddiq is a description of one who speaks truth often and combines truth with truth in belief in Allah, exalted is He, and His messengers, so by this they become witnesses over others.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿and the martyrs﴾ is not coordinated upon what preceded; rather it is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His saying ﴿with their Lord﴾, or that [phrase] is a qualifier and its predicate is His saying ﴿for them is their reward﴾. On this view they differed about what is meant by the martyrs. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: they are the prophets, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41]. Muqatil and Muhammad ibn Jarir said: the martyrs are those who were killed in the way of Allah. It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "What do you count as martyrs among you?" They said: "The one who is killed." He said: "Indeed, the martyrs of my nation would then be few." Then he mentioned that the one killed is a martyr, the one with a stomach ailment is a martyr, and the one who dies of plague is a martyr," and so on in the hadith.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the condition of the believers, He followed it with mention of the condition of the disbelievers, so He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the blazing fire.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verse 20:

When He had mentioned the states of the believers and the disbelievers, He then mentioned what indicates the lowliness of this world and the perfection of the state of the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement, adornment and boasting among you, and competition in wealth and children, like the example of a rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers; then it dries up, and you see it turning yellow, then it becomes debris. And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment, and forgiveness from Allah and approval. And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: The primary purpose of the verse is to belittle the state of this world and to magnify the state of the Hereafter. He said: the world is play, amusement, adornment and boasting. There is no doubt that these things are belittled matters. As for the Hereafter, it is either severe, lasting punishment or the approval of Allah on the basis of permanence, and there is no doubt that this is great.

The second issue: Know that the life of this world is wisdom and rightness. For this reason, when the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], He said: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Had it not been wisdom and rightness, He would not have said that. Also, life is His creation, as He said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. He does not act in vain, as He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115], and He said: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and that between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27]. Also, life is a blessing, indeed it is the root of all blessings, and the realities of things do not differ whether they are in this world or in the Hereafter. Also, He, the Exalted, magnified the favour of bestowing life, so He said: ﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. So the first of the kinds of His blessings that He mentioned is life. What we have mentioned together indicates that the life of this world is not blameworthy. Rather, the intended meaning is that whoever diverts this worldly life not toward obedience to Allah but toward obedience to Satan and pursuit of desire, that is what is blameworthy. Then, the Exalted described it with several attributes:

The first of them: that it is ﴿play (la'ib)﴾, which is the act of children who exhaust themselves greatly, and then those exertions end without any benefit.

The second: that it is ﴿amusement (lahw)﴾, which is the act of young men. Usually, after it ends, nothing remains but regret, because the sensible person, after it ends, sees his wealth gone, his life gone, and his pleasure finished, while his soul has increased in longing and thirst for it along with its loss. So the harms are gathered and successive.

The third: that it is ﴿adornment (zinah)﴾, and this is the habit of women, because what is sought from adornment is beautifying the ugly, and building up a structure that is about to become ruin, and striving to complete what is deficient. And it is known that the accidental does not withstand the essential. So when the world is by its very nature perishable and corrupt by its very nature, how can the sensible person be able to remove these corruptions from it? Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is that the disbeliever occupies himself throughout his life with seeking the adornment of this world, without working for the Hereafter. And this is as it has been said:

Your life, O deceived one, is heedlessness and negligence

The fourth: ﴿a boasting (tafakhur) among you﴾ in attributes that are perishable and passing away, and this is either boasting in lineage, or boasting in power, strength and armies, and all of these are gone.

The fifth: His saying: ﴿and competition in wealth and children﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he gathers wealth in the displeasure of Allah, boasts with it over the friends of Allah, and spends it in the things that anger Allah. So it is darknesses, some above others. And there is no way that the followers of worldly people escape these categories. He explained that when the state of this world is not free from these aspects, it is obligatory to turn away from it toward what leads to the building of the Hereafter. Then He, the Exalted, mentioned a parable for this life, so He said: ﴿like the example of a rain (ghayth)﴾, meaning rain. Its counterpart is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And present to them the example of the life of this world: it is like water﴾ [al-Kahf: 45]. The kaf in His saying ﴿like the example of a rain﴾ is in the nominative case for two reasons:

One of them: that it is an adjective of His saying: ﴿play, amusement, adornment, boasting among you, and competition﴾.

The other: that it is a predicate after a predicate; this was said by al-Zajjaj. And His saying: ﴿whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers﴾ has two opinions:

The first: Ibn Masʿud said: by "the disbelievers" is meant the farmers. Al-Azhari said: the Arabs call the farmer a kafir, because he covers (yakfuru) the seed he sows with the dust of the earth. And when the farmer's vegetation pleases him, together with their knowledge of it, it is at the utmost beauty.

The second: that by "the disbelievers" in this verse is meant the disbelievers in Allah, who are more pleased with the adornment of this world and its tillage than the believers, because they do not see any happiness other than the happiness of this world. His saying ﴿its vegetation (nabatuhu)﴾ means what grew from that rain. The rest of the verse is explained in Surat al-Zumar.

Then He, the Exalted, mentioned after this the state of the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment﴾, meaning for whoever his life was of this description, ﴿and forgiveness from Allah and approval﴾ for His friends and the people of His obedience. This is because, when He described the world with lowliness and swiftness of ending, He made clear that the Hereafter is either lasting severe punishment or approval, which is the greatest of the degrees of reward. Then He said: ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾, meaning for whoever turns toward it and turns away from it in seeking the Hereafter. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the world is the enjoyment of delusion when it distracts you from seeking the Hereafter; but when it calls you to seeking the approval of Allah and seeking the Hereafter, then it is an excellent means.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Race one another to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose breadth is like the breadth of heaven and earth﴾. The meaning is as if He, exalted is He, said: let your boasting and your rivalry be in other than what you are engaged in; rather, be eager that your competition be in seeking the Hereafter.

Know that He, exalted is He, commanded hastening in His saying: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. Then here He explained the manner of that hastening, saying: ﴿Race one another﴾, like the hastening of competitors against their rivals on the racecourse (al-midmar). His saying ﴿to forgiveness﴾ has two issues.

The first issue: There is no doubt that what is meant is hastening toward what brings forgiveness. Some said: what is meant is "race to repentance." Others said: what is meant is "race to all that you have been charged with," so repentance is included in it. This is more correct, because forgiveness and the Garden are not attained except by refraining from all sins and occupying oneself with all acts of obedience.

The second issue: The advocates of the view that a command implies immediacy (al-fawr) argued from this verse. They said: this verse indicates the obligation of hastening, so delay must be forbidden. As for His saying ﴿and a Garden whose breadth is like the breadth of heaven and earth﴾, and in Al 'Imran He said ﴿a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾, they mentioned several opinions about it:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult in what He has given you. And God does not love everyone self-conceited and boastful.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: This lam (the lam of purpose, "so that") indicates making the first part of the speech a cause for the last part, as when you say: "I stood up so that I might strike you." It indicates that standing up is a cause for striking. Here too it is so, because God, exalted is He, has explained that God's information about these things occurring by qada' (divine decree) and qadar (divine measure), and their being recorded in the Book which does not change, necessitates that a person's joy at what has occurred should not intensify, and that his grief at what has not occurred should not intensify. This is what is meant by his, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever knows the secret of God in qadar, calamities become easy for him." The full discussion of this is that, according to the madhhab of the People of the Sunnah, the occurrence of everything that occurred is necessary, and the non-occurrence of everything that did not occur is also necessary, for four reasons:

The first: God, exalted is He, knew its occurrence, so if it did not occur, knowledge would turn into ignorance.

The second: God willed its occurrence, so if it did not occur, the will would turn into mere wishing (tamanni).

The third: God's power was related to bringing it about, so if it did not occur, that power would turn into incapacity.

The fourth: God, exalted is He, decreed its occurrence by His speech, which is truth, so if it did not occur, that true report would turn into falsehood. Therefore, if this that occurred had not occurred, these four attributes would change from perfection to deficiency, and from eternity to createdness. Since that is impossible, we know that there is no repeller of that occurrence. At that point, grief and sorrow disappear upon the manifestation of these thoughts, and trials and calamities become easy for him. As for the Mu'tazilah, suppose they dispute regarding power and will, yet they agree regarding knowledge and goodness. If compulsion (jabr) is necessary in these two attributes, then what difference is there between compulsion arising from these two attributes and compulsion arising from the four attributes? As for the philosophers, compulsion is their doctrine, because they linked the occurrence of human acts to mental conceptions and animal imaginings, then they linked those conceptions and imaginings to the celestial orbits, which have determined courses, and it is impossible for what contradicts them to occur. As for the Dahriyyah, who affirm none of the influences, they must say that the occurrence of events is accidental, and if it is accidental it is not voluntary, so compulsion is necessary. It thus becomes clear that there is no escape from this for any of the sects of rational people, whether they acknowledge it or deny it. This is the explanation of how the People of the Sunnah argue from this verse. The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates the soundness of our doctrine that the servant is able and chooses, and that is from several aspects:

The first: His saying: ﴿so that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾ indicates that God, exalted is He, informed them of those calamities being recorded in the Book only so that they would guard against grief and exultation. Had they not been able to perform those acts, this lam would have no benefit.

The second: This verse indicates that God, exalted is He, does not will that grief and exultation occur from them, and that contradicts the saying of the Mujbirah (compulsionists): that God, exalted is He, willed all of that from them.

The third: He, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿And God does not love everyone self-conceited and boastful﴾, and this indicates that He, exalted is He, does not will that, because love and will are the same. This contradicts the saying of the Mujbirah: that everything that occurs is willed by God, exalted is He.

The fourth: He, exalted is He, introduced the lam of causation before His act with His saying: ﴿so that not﴾, and this indicates that the acts of God, exalted is He, are causally motivated by purpose. I say: The rational person is greatly amazed at how these verses relate to compulsion and divine decree, and how both groups attach themselves to most of them.

The second issue: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Abu 'Amr alone read: "bima ataakum" (with qasr, short alif), and the rest read: "atakum" (with madd, long alif). The argument of the rest is that when it is lengthened (madd), that is attributed to God, exalted is He, who is the Giver of that, and the subject of the verb in ﴿ataakum﴾ is a pronoun returning to the name of God, glorified and exalted is He, and the ha' is omitted from the relative clause; its estimate is: "bima ataakumuhu" (with what He gave you).

Rather its meaning is: do not grieve to the degree that drives you to destroy yourselves, and do not count on reward for the loss of what was taken from you; and do not exult with an intense joy that makes you rebellious until you become insolent and arrogant in it. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God does not love everyone self-conceited﴾, so this indicates that He dispraised the joy in which its possessor becomes conceited and arrogant, whereas joy in God's blessing and thanks for it is not blameworthy. All of this is the meaning of what Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "No one is without joy and grief, but make patience your response to calamity and thankfulness your response to good." The judge (al-Qadi) argued from this verse that God, exalted is He, does not will the acts of the servants. (The reply to this is that) many of our companions distinguished between love and will, and said: love is a specific kind of will, namely the will of reward, so negating this will does not necessitate negating absolute will.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people. And whoever turns away—indeed, God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding the verse there are two opinions:

The first: This is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿every arrogant boaster﴾, as if He had said: He does not love the arrogant, nor does He love those who are stingy, meaning those who rejoice with exultant joy. When they are granted wealth and a share of this world, out of their love for it and their attachment to it, they are stingy with it. It is not enough for them that they are stingy with it; rather, they enjoin people to be stingy with it too. All of this is the result of their rejoicing when they attain it. Then He said after that: ﴿And whoever turns away﴾ from the commands and prohibitions of God and does not refrain from what He has forbidden, namely grief over what has been lost and rejoicing in what has come, then indeed God is free of need of him.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿Those who are stingy﴾ is a new, independent statement with no connection to what precedes it. It concerns the description of those who concealed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and were stingy in making known his attributes. Its predicate (khabar) is omitted, and what indicates it is His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away—indeed, God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾ The omission of the predicate is common in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be moved﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31].

The second issue: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi (Abu ʿAli al-Fārisī) said: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited: "fa-inna Allāha al-Ghaniyyu al-Ḥamīd" (فَإنَّ اللَّهَ الغَنِيُّ الحَمِيدُ), omitting the word "huwa" (هو), and likewise it is so in the codices of the people of Medina and Syria. The rest recited: ﴿huwa al-Ghaniyyu al-Ḥamīd﴾ (هُوَ الغَنِيُّ الحَمِيدُ). Abu 'Ali said: It is appropriate that "huwa" in this verse is a separator (fasl, a pronoun of separation) and not a subject (mubtada'), because the separator is easier to omit. Do you not see that it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis), and it may be omitted without harming the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and offspring﴾ [al-Kahf: 39].

The third issue: His saying ﴿indeed, God is huwa the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾ means that God is self-sufficient, so no harm returns to Him from the stinginess of that miser. His saying ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ is as if it were an answer to a question that arises here, for it may be asked: Since He, exalted is He, knew that he would be stingy with that wealth and would not spend it on the ways of obedience, why did He give him that wealth? The answer is that He, exalted is He, is praiseworthy in that giving, and deserving of praise in that He opened for him the doors of His mercy and blessing. If the servant falls short in obedience, then its burden returns to him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verse 25 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾. Regarding the interpretation of "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat), there are two views.

The first, which is the view of Muqatil ibn Sulayman, is that they are the evident miracle and the overpowering proofs.

The second, which is the view of Muqatil ibn Hayyan, is that they are the deeds that call them to obedience to God and to turning away from other than God. The first is the correct view, because their prophethood was established only through those miracles.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the Balance, that people may uphold justice. And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for people﴾.

Know that the parallel of this verse is His saying: ﴿God is He who sent down the Book with truth and the Balance﴾ [al-Shura: 17], and He said: [p. 210] ﴿And the heaven He raised and set up the Balance﴾. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning the connection between the Book, the Balance and the iron, there are several aspects.

One of them, and this is what I say, is that the basis of legal responsibility (al-taklif) rests on two matters:
One: doing what ought to be done.
Two: abandoning what ought to be abandoned.
The first is the primary objective, because if the primary objective were abstention, it would follow that no one should be created, since abstention was already present in eternity. As for doing what ought to be done, it is either related to the soul, which is knowledge (al-ma'arif), or to the body, which is the actions of the limbs. The Book is that by which one reaches doing what ought to be done among the inner acts, so that truth may be distinguished from falsehood and proof from doubt. The Balance is that by which one reaches doing what ought to be done among the bodily acts, for most of the heavy obligations in actions concern dealing with creatures, and the Balance is that by which justice is distinguished from injustice and the excess from the deficiency. As for iron, in it is great might, and it deters creatures from what ought not to be done. The sum is that the Book refers to the theoretical faculty, the Balance to the practical faculty, and iron to the repelling of what ought not to be done. Since the noblest of the divisions is the preservation of spiritual interests, then the preservation of bodily interests, then the restraint from what ought not to be done, this order has been observed in this verse.

Second: dealing is either with the Creator, and its path is the Book, or with creatures, and these are either loved ones, and dealing with them is on equal terms, which is by the Balance, or enemies, and dealing with them is by the sword and iron.

Third: people are of three kinds. Either they are the foremost (al-sabiqun), who deal with creatures according to what the Book requires, so they are fair and do not seek to be vindicated, and they avoid the places of doubt. Or they are the moderate (al-muqtasidun), who are fair and also seek their own rights, so they need the Balance. Or they are the wrongdoers (al-zalimun), who seek their rights but are not fair, and they need iron and deterrence.

Fourth: the human being is either in the station of truth, which is the station of the tranquil soul (al-nafs al-mutma'inna) and the station of those brought near, so here he does not rest except in God and acts only by the Book of God, as He said: ﴿Verily, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. Or he is in the station of the path (al-tariqa), which is the station of the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwama) and the station of the companions of the right, so he needs the Balance in knowing the moral qualities, so that he guards against the two extremes of excess and deficiency and remains upon the straight path. Or he is in the station of the Law (al-shari'a), which is the station of the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammara), and here he needs the iron of struggle and severe disciplines.

Fifth: the human being is either one who possesses unveiling and arrival, so he has no intimacy except with the Book, or one who seeks and reasons, so he needs the Balance of proof and argument, or one who is stubborn and contentious, so he must be removed from the earth by iron.

Sixth: religion is either fundamentals (al-usul) or branches (al-furu'). In other words, it is either knowledge or actions. The fundamentals come from the Book. As for the branches, the aim is the acts in which lies their justice and their welfare, and this is by the Balance, for it is an indication of the observance of justice, and iron is for disciplining whoever abandons these two paths.

Seventh: the Book refers to the rulings God mentioned in His Book which require justice and equity, and the Balance refers to compelling people to those rulings founded on justice and equity, and this is the task of kings. Iron refers to the fact that if they rebel, they must be compelled to these two by the sword. This indicates that the rank of the scholars, who are the masters of the Book, is higher than the rank of the kings, who are the masters of the sword. The aspects of connection are many, and what we have mentioned points to the rest.

The second issue: concerning the sending down of the Balance and the sending down of iron, they mentioned two views.

The first: that God, exalted is He, sent them down from heaven. It is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) descended with the Balance and gave it to Nuh (Noah), and said: "Command your people to weigh with it." And it is reported from Ibn Abbas: Adam descended from the Garden with five things of iron: the anvil (al-sandan), the pincers (al-kalbatan), the hammer (al-miqmaʿa), the mallet (al-mitraqa), and the needle. The miqmaʿa is what is used for sharpening. Something that confirms the soundness of this is what Ibn Umar narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God, exalted is He, sent down four blessings from heaven to earth: iron, fire, water and salt."

The second view: the meaning of this sending down is creation and preparation, like His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Qutrub said: "We sent them down" means "We prepared them," from the word nuzul (provision of hospitality), as one says: "The governor provided a fine hospitality (nuzul) to so-and-so." Some of them said: this is of the same kind as the saying: "I fed it straw and cold water, and I ate bread and milk."

The third issue: it has been mentioned regarding the benefits of the Balance that people may uphold justice. Qist (al-qist) and iqsat mean equity, which is that you give another his share just as you take your own share, and the just person is muqsit. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God loves the equitable﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42]. As for iron, in it is great might, for instruments of war are made from it. And in it are also many benefits, among them His saying: ﴿And We taught him the making of armour for you﴾ [al-Anbiya': 80]. Among them is that the interests of the world are either fundamentals or branches. The fundamentals are four: agriculture, weaving, building houses, and rulership (al-saltana). This is because a human being is compelled to food that he eats, clothing that he wears, and a dwelling in which he sits, and the human being is civic by nature, so his welfare is not complete except when a group of his kind gathers, each one of whom occupies himself with a particular important matter. Then the interests of all are organized by all, and that organization must lead to competition, and there must be a person who repels the harm of some from others, and that is the sultan. Thus it is established that the interest of the world is not organized except by these four letters.

As for agriculture, it needs iron, for ploughing and digging the lands. Then, when these grains come into being and grow, they must be threshed and cleaned, and this is not completed except by iron. Then the grains must be ground, and this is not completed except by iron. Then they must be baked, and this is not completed except by fire, and there must be an iron flint. As for fruits, they must be cleaned of their peels and cut in the forms suitable for eating, and this is not completed except by iron. As for weaving, it is known that the tools of weaving need iron, and then cutting and sewing garments needs iron. As for building, it is known that the perfection of the matter there is not achieved except by iron. As for the means of rulership, it is known that they are not completed or perfected except by iron. At this point it becomes clear that most of the interests of the world are not completed except by iron. It also becomes clear that gold cannot take the place of iron in any of these interests. Were gold not found in the world, nothing of the interests of the world would be disrupted, but were iron not found, all the interests of the world would be disrupted.

Then, since the need for iron is intense, He made it easy to find and abundant in existence, while gold, since the need for it is little, He made rare in existence. At this point the effect of God's generosity and mercy upon His servants becomes manifest, for everything whose need is greater, He made its finding easier. For this reason some of the wise said: the thing most needed is air, for if its arrival to the heart were cut off for a moment, the human being would die at once. Therefore God made it the easiest of things to find, and prepared the means and instruments of breathing, so that a human being breathes constantly by the demand of his nature, without needing to exert effort. After air comes water, but since the need for water is less than the need for air, He made obtaining water slightly harder than obtaining air. After water comes food, and since the need for food is less than the need for water, He made obtaining food harder than obtaining water. Then foods differ in degrees of need and rarity, so whatever its need is greater, its finding is easier, and whatever its finding is more difficult, its need is less. As for jewels, since the need for them is very little, they are therefore very rare. Thus we know that whatever the need for a thing is greater, its finding is easier. And since the need for God's mercy, exalted is He, is greater than the need for everything else, we hope from His bounty that He will make it the easiest of things to find. The poet said:

Glory be to Him who singled out the Mighty with His might,
while people are in need of none of His kind.
He made the breaths of air humble, and every soul
is in need of His breaths.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that God may know who helps Him and His messengers in the unseen. Indeed God is Strong, Mighty﴾. Concerning this there are issues.

The first issue: the meaning is "that God may know who helps Him," that is, who helps His religion and helps His messengers by using swords, spears and all weapons in striving against the enemies of the religion "in the unseen," that is, while absent from them. Ibn Abbas said: they help Him without seeing Him. Close to this is His saying: ﴿If you help God, He will help you﴾ [Muhammad: 7].

The second issue: one who holds that God's knowledge is originated (muhdath) argues from His saying: "that God may know." The answer to this is that He, exalted is He, intended by knowledge the object of knowledge (al-ma'lum). It is as if He said: "so that the help of the Messenger, peace be upon him, may take place from those who help him."

The third issue: al-Jubba'i said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that people may uphold justice﴾ indicates that He sent down the Balance and iron, and that His purpose from the servants is that they uphold justice and help the Messenger. If this is His purpose from all of them, then the statement of the Mujbira (the determinists) that He intended from some of them the opposite of that has been refuted.

(Its answer): How is it possible that He intends that from all of them while He knows that its opposite exists, and that combining opposites is impossible, and that the impossible is not intended?

The fourth issue: since help may be apparent, as happens from a hypocrite or from one whose aim is worldly benefit, God, exalted is He, clarified that what He intended is help "in the unseen," and its meaning is that it occurs out of sincerity in the heart. Then God, exalted is He, clarified that He is powerful over affairs and mighty, not to be opposed.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 57, verse 25 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham, and placed in their offspring prophethood and the Scripture﴾. Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He sent the messengers with clear proofs and miracles, and that He sent down the balance (mizan) and iron, and commanded the creation to stand by supporting them, He followed that with an explanation of the other favours He bestowed upon them. He explained that He, exalted is He, honoured Noah and Abraham, peace be upon them both, with messengership. Then He placed in their offspring prophethood and the Scripture. Thus, no one came after them bearing prophethood except that he was from their descendants. He mentioned prophethood before the Scripture because the perfection of the state of a prophet is that he becomes one who possesses a Scripture and a law (shar').

Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Among them are those who are guided, but many of them are defiant sinners﴾, and in this there are issues:

First issue: "Among them are those who are guided," i.e., among the offspring (dhurriyyah) or among those to whom the messengers were sent. The mention of sending and the messengers indicates them. The meaning is that among them there are those who are guided and among them there are those who are defiant (fasiq), and the majority are defiant. Regarding the word "fasiq" here there are two opinions:

The first: it refers to one who has committed a major sin (kabirah), whether he was a disbeliever or not, because this term is applied to the disbeliever and to one who is not, likewise when he has committed a major sin.

The second: the intended meaning of "fasiq" here is the disbeliever, because the verse indicates that He, Exalted is He, made the defiant ones the opposite of those who are guided, so it is as if the meaning is that among them are those who accepted the religion and were guided, and among them are those who did not accept and were not guided. It is known that whoever is like this is a disbeliever. But this is weak, because the Muslim who disobeyed may also be described as not having been guided to the right path of his religion.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent, following in their footsteps, Our messengers, and We sent after them Jesus, son of Mary, and gave him the Injil﴾, and in this there are two issues:

First issue: the meaning of "qaffa" is that he followed after another who had passed away. The intended meaning is that Allah, Exalted is He, sent some of them after others until it reached the days of Jesus, peace be upon him, so Allah sent him after them and gave him the Injil.

Second issue: Ibn Jinni said: al-Hasan recited "wa-atayna-hu al-Anjil" with a fatha on the hamza. Then he said: this is a pattern with no parallel, because af'il, in their view, is from najaltu al-shay' when you extract it, because rulings are extracted by it; and the Torah is fawalah from warā al-zand yarī when it produces fire; and similar to it is al-Furqan, which is fu'lan from farraqtu bayn al-shay'ayn. Accordingly, it is not permissible to put a fatha on the hamza, because it has no parallel. The strong assumption is that he did not recite it except by transmission, and it has two possible explanations:

One of them: it is an anomalous reading (shadhdh), as some have related concerning "al-bartil."

The second: he thought the Injil was a foreign word, so he altered its pattern to point out that it is foreign.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy, and monasticism which they invented﴾, and in this there are issues:

First issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) have used this verse to argue that the act of the servant is a creation of Allah, Exalted is He, and an acquisition (kasb) of the servant. They said: because He, Exalted is He, has ruled that these things are placed by Allah, Exalted is He, and has ruled that they invented that monasticism. The Qadi said: the intended meaning of this is that He, Exalted is He, showed them kindness until their motives to monasticism grew strong, which is bearing the additional hardship beyond what is obligatory, such as seclusion and coarse clothing.

(The answer): this is abandoning the apparent meaning without evidence. Moreover, even if we grant that, it also achieves our aim; for in a state of equal balance (istiwa') it is impossible for a preponderance to occur, otherwise a preponderance has occurred at equal balance, and combining the two is contradictory. And if occurrence at equal balance is impossible, then at the state of being outweighed it is even more fitting that it be impossible. And if the outweighed option is impossible, the preponderant option is necessary, since there is no exit from the two extremes of a contradiction.

Second issue: Muqatil said: the intended meaning of "ra'fah" and "rahmah" is that they were affectionate toward one another, just as Allah described the companions of Muhammad, peace be upon him, with this in His saying: ﴿compassionate among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

Third issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it was recited as "ra'afah" on the pattern fa'alah.

Fourth issue: "rahbaniyyah" means the act attributed to the monks (ruhban), and the monk is one who fears; it is fa'lan from rahiba, like khashyan from khashiya. It was also recited "wa-ruhbaniyyah" with a damma, as if it were a relative noun to ruhban, which is the plural of rahib, like rakib and rukban,

and the intended meaning of "rahbaniyyah" is their practice of monasticism in the mountains, fleeing from tribulation in religion, dedicating themselves to worship, and bearing hardships beyond the acts of worship that were obligatory upon them, namely seclusion, coarse clothing, withdrawal from women, and worship in caves and grottoes. From Ibn Abbas: in the period of interruption (fatrah) between Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, the kings altered the Torah and the Injil, so a people wandered the earth and wore wool. Ibn Mas'ud related that he, peace be upon him, said: "O Ibn Mas'ud, do you not know that the Children of Israel split into seventy sects, all of them in the Fire except three sects: a sect that believed in Jesus, peace be upon him, and fought the enemies of Allah in his support until they were killed; a sect that had no capacity for fighting, so they enjoined good and forbade evil; and a sect that had no capacity for either of the two, so they wore cloaks and went out to the deserts and wastelands, and this is His saying: ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion﴾ to the end of the verse."

Fifth issue: Allah, Exalted is He, did not intend by "they invented it" the manner of blame; rather the intended meaning is that they introduced it from their own selves and abandoned it; for this reason He, Exalted is He, said after it: ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾.

Sixth issue: "wa-rahbaniyyatan" is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb that the apparent verb explains; its estimate is: "they invented a monasticism which they invented." Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "rahbaniyyah" cannot be construed as the object of "ja'alna" (We placed), because what they invent cannot be something made by Allah, Exalted is He. I say: this statement is complete only if it is established that a created thing being between two capable agents is impossible; and how is it fitting for Abu Ali to delve into such matters?

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾, meaning We did not impose it on them.

As for His saying: ﴿except the seeking of God's good pleasure﴾, there are two views:

The first: it is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception where what follows is not of the same category as what precedes). The meaning is: "But they invented it, seeking God's good pleasure."

The second: it is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*, an exception where what follows belongs to the same category as what precedes). The meaning is: "We did not impose it upon them except in the manner of seeking God's good pleasure." The intent is that it was not obligatory, for the purpose of performing an obligatory act is to avert punishment and attain God's pleasure, whereas the purpose of performing a recommended act is not to avert punishment, but rather its purpose is nothing other than attaining God's good pleasure.

As for God's saying: ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, there are several views:

The first: those who invented this monasticism (*rahbaniyyah*) did not observe it with its proper observance. Rather, they added to it the doctrine of the Trinity and incarnation. Some of them remained upon the religion of 'Isa (Jesus) until they reached Muhammad (ﷺ) and believed in him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾.

The second: We did not prescribe that monasticism for them except so that they might draw near to God's good pleasure by it. Then they did perform those acts, but not for this purpose; rather for another purpose, namely seeking worldly gain, ostentation and reputation.

The third: when We prescribed it for them, they abandoned it, and this would be a reproach to them insofar as they abandoned an obligation.
